responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Two-Plus-One Brief Psychotherapy: A Response to Michael Barkham and Bob Hobson

Barbara Dick

Barbara Dick

Barbara Dick  

Michael Barkham's and Bob Hobson's papers in the journal on the rationale of the Two Plus One model of psychotherapy and the account of the therapy with a patient clarified for me a major difference in stance and attitude between my understanding of dynamic psychotherapy, whether radical or conservative, and that of the two authors. It seems to me that this therapy is essentially behavioural and directive, and that this has major implications in terms of Barkham's proposition that the model will ‘enable investigations to be made on psychodynamic processes which will be technically heightened by the short duration of therapy’. Psychotherapy research needs to address itself to defining accurately the nature of the processes that are involved if any general conclusions of value are to be drawn. The assessment of the effectiveness of any model of psychotherapy needs to compare and contrast and to define difference in relation to other models.

For more than thirty years I worked with Brief Psychotherapy, as it is now called, in the NHS using the Jungian analytic approach in individual and group analytic therapy. My experience does not suggest that patient satisfaction evaluates therapy as Barkham seems to suggest in quoting Silverman and Beech, nor that single session improvement of necessity tells us much of what has taken place for post hoc is not as we all know propter hoc. Kate Wooff and I (Dick & Wooff 1986) followed up patients who were admitted to a time-limited programme of twelve weeks of group psychotherapy, and found that those who dropped out of the therapy expressed as much satisfaction with their life situation as the the full participators in the therapy. This was surprising in view of the fact that the drop-outs had significantly increased their use of the inpatient, out-patient and day-patient psychiatric services compared with the year prior to their admission to the Wilton Unit. This was in contrast to those who completed therapy, the majority of whom had had little or no use of the psychiatric services in the year following admission. We concluded from this unexpected finding that both users of the therapy and the non-users found the outcome of their admission to the Unit satisfactory for them. Both groups would appear to have accepted their current status. Those who had participated in the psychotherapy and were no longer patients three years after admission were satisfied with the change of status whilst the drop-outs who continued with the status of patient appeared satisfied to remain in a treatment situation more appropriate to their mental state.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

It proved popular to have a previous section of poems; at least it was popular with other poets who subsequently submitted many poems. We have selected four poets in this issue. As we have previously mused (Editorial, Winter 88-89), the nature of human expression has separate forms, but the boundaries between each are fuzzy.

The comment by Whyte on causation and disposition reminds us of this distinction, and that its problems do not just go away. Jeremy Holmes' Lecture for the Journal last May, which we publish in this issue of the Journal, is a view from the country; a more leisurely amble through the territory that might become a civil war between the two cultures of science and literature. The values inherent in human relationships and in self-appraisal are not simply translatable into those of impartial science and the investigations of causation. The values of working with human beings are to be found in those of human association: social values. In a detailed argument Jeremy Holmes has pointed to how the ingredients of psychoanalytic psychotherapy can be expressed in social values of assimilation, pluralism, irony and imagery (the transformational image).

Nathan Field also wishes to draw our attention to a similar correspondence. He has neatly demonstrated the way in which the apparently scientific approaches to the positive and negative transferences which characterise different schools of analytic psychotherapy can be understood equally in terms of healing and exorcism respectively.

It is not possible to write about, nor read about, child sexual abuse without a rising indignation, a moral reaction that is not part of rational science but which is nevertheless the essence of the problem of child abuse. We cannot divorce a human reaction from our scientific awareness. As Whyte indicates, and as Fiona Gardner ruthlessly pursues, the question of moral and social values persists right into the therapeutic session and is the core of the transference/counter-transference creation. In the latter paper, Fiona Gardner shows that the issues of child sexual abuse are impaled uncomfortably on the issues of social stereotypes, which determine the character of the therapist/patient interactions as much as the forms of the sexual abuse.

[[RunningHead]]

Understanding Women in Distress by Pamela Ashurst and Zaida Hall. Published by Tavistock/Routledge: London, 1989; x + 237 pages; £12.95 paperback.

Kate Osborne

Kate Osborne

Kate Osborne  

Despite powerful myths to the contrary, no man has ever experienced pregnancy, childbirth, lactation, nor even the regular monthly rhythm of menstruation. Yet whenever anything goes wrong with any of these processes (and even when they are working well as in a healthy pregnancy), women are invariably confronted with male experts who have to make great empathic leaps in order to understand, diagnose and treat. This book is written principally in an attempt to enlighten male medical colleagues, whether they be GPs, gynaecologists/obstetricians, psychiatrists or others who are consulted by women when ill or in distress.

For the authors, women's biology clearly affects their destiny since the focus is on distress caused by women's reproductive processes throughout the life cycle. The book begins with an outline of how early childhood experiences affect the way in which we respond to life's vicissitudes as adults, giving in simple language an object-relations account of emotional distress. Pamela Ashurst and Zaida Hall then go on to consider the position of women in society, giving a brief historical analysis of women's oppression in patriarchy and the way this influences feminine identity and sexuality. Dinora Pines contributes a chapter on her psychodynamic understanding of the transition to motherhood, which is complemented by the authors with a chapter on women's common reactions to their babies.

The scene is then set to consider, in the following 15 chapters, selected issues which underlie the crises that are likely to affect women today. They begin with an analysis of the eating disorders commonly seen in adolescent girls, followed by a particularly sympathetic chapter on childhood sexual abuse. This includes a short outline of the presenting symptoms which should alert practitioners to the possibility of sexual, especially incestuous, abuse. Interestingly, there is no chapter developing the earlier comments made about female sexuality despite the lengthy post-Lacanian debate about women's autosexuality and the large numbers of women expressing dissatisfaction with their sexual experiences. However, they do provide a non-pathologising account of lesbian womanhood which may help to counterbalance the homophobic accounts found in standard psychiatric and medical texts.

Psychotherapist's Creed

Robin Higgins and Robert Rentoul

Robert Rentoul

Robert Rentoul  

Dear Sir

When I received the Autumn 1989 issue of the British Journal of Psychotherapy and looked through it briefly about two months ago, I felt offended by The Psychotherapist's Creed printed on page 120. I started to write to you to say so, but decided to let it lie - I think because I didn't want to appear unduly touchy.

However, I have now read through the Journal from the beginning, and have again arrived at page 120: and again I feel offended. I feel that it is thoroughly inappropriate for the pages of a professional journal It may be clever, but in so far as this is because of its close verbal parallelism to the Christian Apostles' Creed, it is that which makes it particularly offensive.

I am sorry that this should be my first letter to you about the Journal, for I have welcomed it from the beginning and appreciate it.

Robert Rentoul

Journal of Analytical Psychology, Volume 35, Number 3, 1990

The Burning Cauldron: Transference as Paradox

C. Savitz

This paper is a consideration of the transference as paradox - as an experience of irreconcilable meanings and unresolved contradictions. Many of the metaphors in the analytic field refer to the holding function of the transference and do not address the underlying tension and paradox of analysis - that the content affirms what the form denies. I have used the image of Dionysus, the dismembered child, as the embodiment of paradox and have identified the recognition of paradox and ambiguity as one of the goals of the analytic process. In addition, I have reconsidered Winnicott's understanding of transitional phenomena in the light of the more ambivalent concept of liminality and used my work with a schizoid patient to illustrate how the traumatised psyche takes flight from paradox and is forced to reencounter paradox in the transference.



British Journal of Medical Psychology, Volume 62, Part 4, 1989

Damaged Identity and the Search for Kinship in Adult Adoptees

Heather Humphrey and Michael Humphrey

A postal questionnaire was sent to 100 members of an organization for helping adopted individuals to trace their origins. Replies were received from 42 women and 34 men, some of whom were interviewed in person or more often by telephone. The voyage of self-discovery was evidently more crucial for women, whose need for a stronger sense of identity had been enhanced by marriage and motherhood.

Relatively more men than women had sought help for personal problems in adulthood, although paradoxically more women reported an unhappy experience of adoption and a damaged sense of identity. Predictably, mother-child reunions had often proved disappointing and occasionally distressing for both parties. In contrast, the discovery of lost siblings had usually brought more reward. This aspect of the search for biological relatives deserves more emphasis, in case adoptees (especially when reared as only children and/or when pyschologically disturbed) might have more to gain from meeting a sibling than from meeting a parent.

Psychotherapists against Nuclear Disaster

Diana Priestley

Diana Priestley

Diana Priestley  

Dear Editor

PAND continues its task of keeping alive and public the contribution that psychoanalytical thinking has to make to issues of war and peace, both by meeting together, and by offering workshops or groups to large conferences on disarmament and related issues. We have made links with other professional groups using their skills to further understanding in this field.

PAND members ran a large group at the Medical Campaign Against Nuclear Arms conference last autumn and home groups are being organised at this year's Symposium - Health and Security 2000 - New Thinking in Europe. This marks the 10th Anniversary of the Medical Campaign and International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War. Links have been made with SPINA (Study Group for Psychosocial Issues in Nuclear Arms) and PWDD - Professions for World Disarmament and Development.

Our Autumn workshop with Scilla Elworthy, Director of the Oxford Research Group, had as its theme - The Decision Machine - and focused on the attitudes and assumptions of decision makers in the field of nuclear arms.

New members are very welcome and should contact the Administrative Secretary on 071 928 5747.

Diana Priestley

Commentary by an Analytical Psychotherapist

Jean Scarlett

Jean Scarlett

Jean Scarlett  

The essence of this therapy is, in Winnicott's terms, the creation of a good enough mother/child relationship and the sensitive therapist seems intuitively to appreciate this. Many of the transactions and interpretations, whatever their immediate implications, must be seen in this overall context. However, let us first consider one or two of the more obvious conflicts with which the therapist is rightly dealing as she allows them to arise in their own way and time and then moves on to the very difficult issues which may eventually confront her. (I find I think of the therapist as ‘she’.)

From the description of the patient and her history, certain particulars stand out, notably the very early separations from her mother and their disturbing repercussions. In the transference area, we note the immediate substitution of the therapy for the relationship with the boy friend. Although the holiday is presumably by mutual agreement, the patient feels she is being deserted by her therapist. This emerges clearly by implication in what she says in the first session about her friend F, who may be pregnant, which means she will have less time to spend with Helen. As the therapist points out, this makes her feel like ‘a child displaced’. These feelings were also experienced in relation to other friends, towards her sister when she married and towards her boy friend. As the therapist says, the fear is of total abandonment like that which took place in infancy. Apt though the interpretation doubtless is, I think that F's pregnancy may have further significance which may become apparent or which may need facilitation. For one thing, Helen's depression at the news of F's pregnancy may be connected with her own frustrated maternal feelings or with an unconscious fear, dating from one of the separation periods, that the absent mother had not only rejected her but gone away to produce another baby to usurp Helen's place - a not infrequent fantasy in such cases.

The second session begins with a good deal of latent rage. Some of this rage is projected on to the difficult store lady who comes to ‘sort’ her out. This phrase connects the store lady with the therapist whose role is to sort out Helen's problems but, owing to its colloquial meaning, also implies that at some level Helen thinks of her as critical. Helen is also identified with the very sick patients for whom the store lady/therapist sometimes fails to provide ‘things’.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

American psycho-analysis has been in a deepening crisis for a decade or two. Much of the problem seems to have been the considerable emphasis on the ‘ego’ as a phenomenon objectively observed by the analyst. This reduced psycho-analytic understanding, in the literature at least, to rather mechanistic formulations of the psycho-economics of the ego. And it happens, of course, in the presence of a feeling patient who has a subjective experience of himself and what is going on with him during his analysis. The tendency to displace subjectivity from psycho-analysis, however buttressed by specific selections of Freud's writings, must result in an increasing tension within the profession itself. The result has been two developments: Firstly an antagonistic move against psycho-analysis as too deeply flawed to continue taking seriously, and the consequent development of humanistic psychologies, alternative therapies and latterly integrative attempts to rescue something of psychoanalysis. Secondly there has been a continuing struggle within American psychoanalysis to rescue something of the patient's subjectivity through ‘humanising’ psychoanalysis (e.g. Fromm 1971, The Crisis of Psycho-Analysis; Bettelheim 1983, Freud and Man's Soul); and to change its direction towards the experiencing self and not just the functioning ego.

It is the internal contradiction within Freud's writings and the contradiction within American psycho-analysis which Susan Kelen addresses. The developing psychology of the 'self (Kohut's self-psychology) contrasts with the mechanistic psychology of the ego (ego-psychology). Kelen gives an important survey, for British-trained psychotherapists and psycho-analysts, of the development of the ideas of the 'self in American psychoanalysis, and trains our attention on the way in which a bridge could be built between the ego as, subject and as an object of study.

The issues seem of rather less direct concern for British psychotherapists as the neglect of the subjective 'self has never been so great in British psycho-analysis. Nevertheless we read a good deal about self-psychology and Kohut is popular on reading lists. Kelen's paper gives us an idea of why he writes with his particularly sympathetic approach. His reactive re-emphasis on the feeling subject in the material so often seems squeezed aside in American psycho-analytic literature. Also we have a chance to understand one of the impulsions behind some of the humanistic psychologies and therapies that have been regularly sweeping up on our shores. Their frequent polemical nature may be disconcerting if their background has not been understood. Liam Clarke describes, through his imagined script, the more ghastly scenes towards which the humanistic approach may appear to point. His bitter humour is a warning of the extremes to which reactive efforts can lead.

[[RunningHead]]

Clinical Commentary X

[This section is a regular feature. A short piece of clinical material from an actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the case. The material has been sent ‘blind’ to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention is to put these commentaries on the same material side by side for comparison of the different approaches and to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice - Ed.]

The Therapist Writes

The Patient

Helen is a 27-year-old unmarried woman who has been in twice weekly therapy for ten months. She is slender, dark-haired, attractive and appears to be about 17. She is and presents herself as a successful, responsible professional in the medical field. Helen had wanted to come into therapy with her boyfriend (they had been seeing each other for three years) because she feared that her total dependence on him was endangering the relationship. He refused and she broke up the relationship a few days later. She felt she needed therapy to sort out why she had been so dependent on him, and why she had continued the relationship when it was making her very unhappy. Her presenting symptoms were fears of being abandoned, her passivity, and of never being able to have a relationship of equals; she saw herself as always being in a kind of daughterfather relationship with boyfriends.

History

She is the youngest of four siblings, (G + 10, B + 8, G + 6). Between Helen and the next youngest her mother had two miscarriages. Helen spent ten days in an incubator and had three periods in hospital for operations on a foot before she was four. She can recall only the last. Her mother was not with her in hospital. It causes her much distress. She has had several dreams which seem to be about her time in hospital.

Helen's brother went to a school for maladjusted children, works in a factory and still lives at home. She says that she and her sisters feel guilty about him; she describes him as the scapegoat for the family problems and is also ashamed that he does a manual job. He was often beaten by their father, and she feels that she should have been able to do something about it. Her father says now that he was jealous of the mother's relationship with the brother. She can recall (four years old) her mother putting all the children in the car and turning up on a woman's doorstep and shouting at her. (She thinks her father had an affair with this woman.) Her parents remained together in what she sees as an unhappy marriage with frequent rows. She describes her father as always having an eye for the girls and her mother as not being very affectionate. Father was the only person safe to be angry with.

Murray Cox

Murray Cox

Murray Cox  

The word ‘Poetics’- in the subtitle of this volume - is much in vogue. The book sits comfortably on my shelves alongside The Poetics of Space and The Poetics of Reverie (Bachelard), A Poetics of Belief (Scott) and Introduction to Poetics (Todorov). There are many more with which I am not at home. And the reader will find that there is more than a clang association to Laing's work The Politics of Experience. Both books are as disturbing as they are intended to be.

The Greek word poiesis is the etymological source of ‘poetics’ and it refers to the process of calling something into existence that was not there before. Thus the creative act of writing a poem, or the newly-minted experience linking reader and listener as a poem is read, are both aspects of the dynamic energy inherent in the word poetics.

And what of the poetics of experience presented to us in this thought-provoking volume Between Psychology and Psychotherapy? Although there are several recent publications which emphasise the subjective nature of psychotherapeutic work, both for patient and therapist, the tripartite structure of his book is unusual. Between the first and third part, called ‘A poetics in practice’ and ‘A discipline of discourse’ respectively, is a section entitled ‘A personal story’. This is a sequence of poetic entries from the author's personal psychic diary written over the space of ten years.

It is when we set such intimate and painfully personal material against sentences which come from a totally different frame of reference - and could be jottings for a potential c.v. - that we realise how this book crosses many traditional boundaries which are normally jealously guarded. There are several realms of discourse and psychological themes where this dysjunction is apparent. By way of illustration I am placing one sentence (page 199) alongside another (page 249). And, having done so, I think the material speaks for itself: ‘… it was the last Thursday in July 1969, 1 was sitting in my room in the Academic Department of Psychiatry at the Middlesex Hospital Medical School, London, where I was then a senior lecturer responsible for the behavioural sciences course for the medical students’; ‘…something like the awful adventure of prayer may be what is required of me. Not the sense of cosy fireside chats with a knee-sized god, but in some more naked wandering in the wilderness, beyond the rush of ordinary things’.

Commentary by a Freudian Child Psychotherapist

Trevor Hartnup

Trevor Hartnup

Trevor Hartnup  

Introduction

I have sympathy and admiration for the therapist in her strenuous attempts to go on working in face of F's difficult and dangerous behaviour and the anger and feelings of abuse that were naturally aroused in her. No differences of view which follow detract from that. It demands the utmost from therapists as professionals and as human beings to process the denigrating behaviour and destructiveness which is directed at them by child patients, concretely not symbolically. In any case I take it that the main purpose of this commentary is to illustrate my own way of thinking about the material.

Immediate Reactions

I would have welcomed a more detailed history including an account of when the behaviour started and whether the parents were being seen - but we often find ourselves wishing we had more information.

The account begins with an impression of instability in F's care situation both in the past and in the present, possibly affecting F's attendance at his session on Friday. Therapy seems to have started in his first year of school. Was this also when the behaviour problems started? Or, as is often the case, did starting at school merely make public a problem which had existed for a long time before that? Loss of a nanny and a new escort - did F have as little warning as his therapist?

F ignores Mrs P. His first reaction to the missed session? Or a habitual beginning? Short sleeves - he strokes his arms and seems to be going to touch Mrs P - this in a boy who exposes himself. It looks as if there may be perverse elements in the transference. In the subsequent verbal abuse and smiling behaviour this impression seems to be confirmed. But it is difficult to evaluate without being there. Is it sadistic or some kind of triumph or what? This scene ‘by the lifts’ is always an awkward one for child psychotherapists. What should be our relationship to the child outside the consulting room? Don recognises that he is still in charge of F.

F's behaviour in the room and his contempt seem to confirm the sadistic element. His glances at Don and Mrs P suggest he wants to see the effect he is having. Is this behaviour a defensive turning passive into active, creating the same feeling of mess and denigration in Mrs P as the various losses (including the gaps between sessions) have produced in him? Or is he attacking because he fears Mrs P will be angry with him about the missed session? Perhaps Mrs P has the transference to the nanny in mind in her interpretation of the ‘rubbish girl’. He may be in some confusion about whether girls are rubbish because they don't stay, or whether they don't stay because he rubbishes them - i.e. they can't stand the rubbish side of him. There is a technical problem here in how to negotiate the sadistic element.

Nathan Field  

When the funeral service for Dr W- was over, five mourners adjourned to the large Victorian pub adjacent to the Crematorium. Although strangers to one another they shared one significant characteristic: each had for many years been in analysis with the late Dr W-. At this hour the upper lounge stood empty and therefore it was possible to speak freely. Mr A-, who had taken the initiative to invite the others, raised his glass in welcome:

‘This is indeed a unique occasion. I confess I find it strange and even moving to meet face to face those whose existence I previously knew of only by the ring of the doorbell or the distant click on the latch. I address you as strangers and yet I am inclined to look on you as members of my family, discovered only in the hour of our bereavement. I -.’

At this point Mr B-, more inclined to argument than sentiment, interrupted him: 'What you say presupposes that you saw the doctor as some sort of parent. Before I am enlisted in a family I had not expected to join, let me hasten to declare that I never did. For me he was always simply the “doctor” and I the “patient”. I brought him my illness, he provided the remedy, and for that I paid him his fee. It was a purely professional arrangement.

‘I am aware,’ he continued, 'that his treatment was of rather a special kind and that the instrument of his cure was neither the knife nor the bottle but word of mouth. By registering precisely the words I used he could identify the submerged areas of my disturbance with the accuracy of an echo sounder. That was his great skill. In my view Dr W- was a man of science who applied a technique according to strict scientific principles. Indeed only with the certainty that derives from the laws of cause and effect can one presume to treat the sick, whether in mind or body.

‘I would remind you that Freud, in his classical papers on technique, compares the analyst to the surgeon and this ideal Dr W- fulfilled in an exemplary fashion. By listening attentively he could discern where my vanity, my self deception, my self indulgence lay encysted and made his incision with unerring accuracy. By incision I am referring to the way his interpretations penetrated to the root of my pathology. He was relentless in forcing me to face the truth. He insisted that before I could ever accept myself as I really was I had to know myself as I was. It proved enormously painful: sometimes I imagined his couch as an operating table; sometimes as an inquisitor's rack; session after session I was stretched upon it while the truth was wrung from me drop by drop. I fought him at every step, but by doing so I discovered I could strike hack yet do him no damage; I could even hate him and still be listened to. In fact, I needed his hate and he had the courage to give it, trusting I had the strength to take it.

The Development of Attachment in Adult Life - the NEWPIN Experiment

Andrea Pound

Andrea Pound

London E1 IBB

Andrea Pound  

Introduction

It is generally agreed that the patterns of secure or anxious attachment observed in young children are relatively stable over time. In reviewing a study of adoption Bowlby states: ‘Findings from this and other studies support the hypothesis that there is a sensitive phase in early life after which development of the capacity to make secure and discriminating attachments becomes progressively more difficult - or, put another way, that the pattern in which a child's attachment behaviour is already organised tends to persist and as he grows older to be modified less and less completely by his current experience’ (Bowlby 1982). This position has been criticised as too pessimistic, for example, by the Clarkes, and various individual case histories do indeed demonstrate the remarkable capacity of children to recover from appalling deprivation and adversity, given sufficiently devoted care (Clarke & Clarke 1976). However, we do not know how these children fared in later life, and in general the outcomes of early loss of attachment figures and the disruption of affectional ties support Bowlby's hypothesis. Children brought up in care, for example, tend to make poor marriages and to have serious difficulties in the care of their own children (Quinton & Rutter 1983). Loss of parents by death or desertion predisposes women to later depression in the context of adversity and negative life events (Brown & Harris 1978). There also appears to be a connection between early loss, particularly that arising from family discord and divorce, and suicide or suicidal attempts (Adam 1982). A number of different patterns have been described, by Bowlby himself and by others, of the later outcomes of early failure in the development of secure attachment. One pattern is that of ‘compulsive independence’ where the individual denies the need for close ties with others, asserts that he faces the world alone and trusts no-one but himself. If this pattern is particularly, though not exclusively, masculine, another, perhaps more typical of women, is of an excessive dependence on others for their inner security, together with a lack of trust in themselves (Bowlby 1977).

Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

If the Standing Conference (UKSCP) shows signs of cohering into a proper professional organisation at last it is because of years of cool (though sometimes impatient) debate. The Conference has become a forum where those who would never normally feel inclined to speak to each other have sat down and shared passionate hopes together. Michael Pokorny's letter, as Chairman of the Conference, marks steady progress in the political organisation of psychotherapy in this country and in Europe.

Politics is one thing; perhaps, however, we are still a long way from a similar engagement over differences of theory and practice. However Petruska Clarkson's careful analysis of the various levels of the psychotherapeutic relationship is an attempt to find a perspective from which an overview might become possible. She contends that all therapeutic relationships have five levels even though the different psychotherapies prioritise different levels. This offers a way of circumventing the inherent contradictions and incompatibilities that exist between different psychotherapies; instead of incompatibilities we have different priorities and emphasis. And this leaves a way open for the beginnings of a possible integration of psychotherapies.

The unusual topic of Cecilia Batten's paper is also one of differences. She emphasises the glancing impact of cultural forces on the relationships both in psychotherapy and in supervision. Such problems are difficult for there is no-one who can stand outside the cross-cultural differences. Our perceptions are all culturally relative whether we are patient, therapist or supervisor.

Nathan Field's imaginative fantasy also dwells on the relativity of our own experiences. He removes us to the gentle methods of ancient Greece, and conveys that there are as many different psychotherapies as there are patients. His plea for diversity within psychotherapy is simply a statement of the uniqueness of experience we each separately possess.

For many of us R D Laing evoked strong but equally contradictory images: guru, psychiatric meddler, social revolutionary and victim of a mind-boggling media career. We publish Joe Berke's brief appreciation of a colleague who could raise psychotherapy and psycho-analysis into a relevant public issue.

Differing Narcissisms

Richard Fry

Richard Fry

Richard Fry  

Dear Sir

In the continuing debate around narcissism I would like to add my observations regarding the writings of the two principal contributors in this field, Kernberg and Kohut. Following on from David Smith's article (British Journal of Psychotherapy, Vol 4(3)) attempting to throw some welcome light on the very confused area that exists in the literature I would like to support his view that most of the writing on this subject can be divided into two camps. However I have found it helpful to think about the position from which these two authorities come.

I recently had occasion to consider the writings of Kernberg and Kohut for the purposes of presenting them to peers for discussion: I came to the subject as a relative ingenue and spent a considerable period wondering why I felt completely confused by what they appeared to be saying, particularly in relation to one another. A number of articles I read drew parallels and highlighted the differences between the two. Clearly there was a large measure of agreement around the concept of the grandiose self, and differences around the areas of development, meaning of the core features, and consequent treatment approaches. Despite this I could not grasp the essential comparisons between them. It was only when I realised that the two authors were not writing within similar frames of reference that I suddenly understood why I had not been able to get my head around the comparisons and the differences.

Kernberg is writing from a firm theoretical base rooted in object relations theory in a direct line of descent. From the theory emerges practice, neatly consequent upon the assumptions underpinning it. Kohut was writing from a position familiar to many, that of the therapist faced with (at first) difficult patient reactions and painful intense countertransference; in other words, the clinical material. From this time-honoured position he attempted to construct an explanatory base for what he intuitively felt was the right approach. As a result his young and inevitably tender theory is vulnerable to attack by intellectual predators, and his writings can sometimes appear difficult to understand in a purely theoretical way. In particular, within the framework of a medical and peri-medical literature he comes over poorly as he is writing within a model that is explicitly at odds with his stated intention of not identifying patients by clusters of recurring symptoms. Kernberg does much better in this setting, of course, and is eloquent in his plea that positive and negative aspects of the transference must be interpreted. Since to neglect this is to condemn the narcissistic patient to increasing fear of the underlying rage and intensify the need for the very defences that cause the problems. Kohut, of course, was trying to stress the phase appropriateness of these patients' demands and insisting that confrontation was just what the doctor didn't order. In order words Kohut and Kernberg are not writing within similar frames of reference but it is often purported that they are. It is therefore difficult and perhaps unwise to see them as in simple opposition to one another.

Michael Pokorny

Michael Pokorny  

As you will see from this newsletter, we have had a busy time since January, and there is no sign of the pace slackening. After a preliminary meeting with Graham Bright MP and Stanley Clinton-Davis the scheduled meeting with the Minister took place and we are now dealing with the letter written to Graham Bright about that meeting. The day before that meeting, I went to the Department of Health to meet the civil servant who advises the Minister and had a meeting which was friendly enough on the surface, but was rather tense and difficult. His basic question was; why should he consider all the varieties of psychotherapy that we represent, rather than sticking to a few well-known brands? We shall answer this in our reply to the Minister's letter. Part of the Council's response is a decision to set up an Audit Sub-Committee which will keep us informed about research in psychotherapy and will initiate a plan for ongoing audit of our members.

I attended the meeting at the House of Commons where the new Minister, Stephen Dorrell, talked to the Parliamentary Group for Complementary Medicine. I was able to get him to confirm that in order to achieve recognition a group should represent the majority of practitioners in the field and should have a coherent policy. This puts emphasis on our need to stick together if we are to achieve recognition as the professional body for psychotherapy.

Dorothy Hamilton and I had a further meeting with Graham Bright and Lord Clinton-Davis in July at which we roughed out a policy for further action and a reply to the ministerial letter. Both are due to be discussed at the meeting of Council on 15 September.

On my daily visits to the office I see a steady stream of letters, notes, etc. Amongst this paperwork there have been two rather alarming items. The first one was a note to say that the DoH is calling a meeting to discuss registration and UKSCP, but not inviting us; the details are in the report of the joint Registration and European Subcommittee. The second one was a letter describing in outline a bill to extend the Data Protection Act to include hand-written records in the same way as computer records. At the time I alerted Lord Clinton-Davis who promptly canvassed support, especially from Lord Ennals, but to no avail. This Bill has now passed through both Houses and got the Royal Assent. From November 1991 all your clients can demand to see your records and you must produce them in full in forty days. This must be of concern to all of us. We shall have to study this Bill and explore its implications.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 71, Part 2, 1990

Can A Liar Be Psychoanalysed?

Edna O'Shaughnessy

At first glance a liar is an inauspicious patient for a psychoanalysis, a treatment based on truthfulness. Because it presents in speech, lying may seem a mature difficulty, but analysis reveals that it is primitive, linked to the habitual liar's doubts and anxieties about communication with primary objects which, from several causes, have become for him lying objects. As expected, lying makes for a series of problems which handicap the analytic process. Even so, the paper illustrates clinically the view that if the fundamental level of the lying that emerges in the analysis is addressed by understanding it as the liar's communication that he is a liar in identification with, and acutely anxious about, his lying object - in the transference the analyst - a genuine analytic process can be set in train.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 71, Part 2, 1990

Pregnancy, Miscarriage and Abortion. A Psychoanalytic Perspective

Dinora Pines

This paper examines some of the unconscious reasons that may lead to unfulfilled pregnancy, either by means of spontaneous abortion, or by conscious planned abortion. During pregnancy the universal dilemma of maternal ambivalence towards the foetus and whom it represents may be strongly influenced by unresolved conflicts and anxieties belonging to earlier stages of a woman's psychic development. Spontaneous or planned abortion, which allows the woman who has become pregnant to deny life to the foetus, may provide a psychosomatic solution to this psychic conflict.

Ambiguity in the Ego: The Basis of the Self in American Psychoanalytic Theory

J. Kelen

J. Kelen

225 Somerset St. West, Suite 201, Ottawa, Ontario, Canada K2P OH7

J. Kelen  

The introduction of 'the self as a psychoanalytic concept in the United States is traced historically to developments in the ego. This article follows the transition in American psychoanalytic theory over a period of forty years, beginning with Anna Freud. These concepts, ‘ego’ and 'self, have been consistently interrelated, as observed in the formulations on narcissism. The impetus was to correct ambiguities that were seen in Freudian theory and to integrate theory and practice. Initially the self was presented as a self-representation (Hartmann 1950, Kohut 1966, Kernberg 1966) and later as a supraordinate structure (Kohut 1977, Kernberg 1982). The formulation of the self within the subjective executive functions of the ego (Kernberg 1982) is suggested to be an attempt to place the self within psychoanalytic theory and resolve the ambiguity in Freud's ego concept. The subjective emotional side of the ego and the objective side which results in identity are addressed while the traditional structural formulation is maintained. The integration of subject and object is consistent with philosophical definitions of the self.

Men and Abuse

Helen Sheldon

Helen Sheldon

Helen Sheldon  

Dear Sir

I would like to comment on the recent paper by David Mann entitled ‘Incest: The Father and The Male Therapist’ (British Journal of Psychotherapy, Vol. 6(2)). Firstly, with regard to a specific point; the author refers to my paper (British Journal of Psychiatry, 1988) and interprets my comments about the therapist's gender as evidence to support his contention that there are positive therapeutic indications for male therapists to work with female incest survivors. I wish to make it clear that I do not agree with Mann concerning this issue. Although the reasons that none of the women in my study first disclosed a history of sexual abuse during the assessment interview could not be specifically correlated with the gender of the therapist (and it was a fairly small sample), I did suggest that the nature of the procedure in itself mitigated against disclosure. Mann clearly does not understand that this must be contextualised within the existing structure of patriarchal NHS institutions which have always medicalised women's psychological distress, thereby maintaining existing power relations and invalidating the reality of incest survivors' experiences. It would seem to me that male therapists can hardly offer an alternative role model to female survivors, whilst continuing to uphold, and act within, the very structures which have not allowed a woman to be the subject of her own story.

Secondly, in focusing on the Oedipal issues facing father and daughter Mann minimises the significance of the basic underlying dynamic operating in childhood sexual abuse, clearly identified by Frosh whose ideas are discussed and then discarded by Mann. Central to this dynamic is the gratification of the perpetrator's need to feel powerful, to feel loved and to release the hostility and frustration for which he has been unable to find appropriate outlets. Although Mann admits to being drawn into this dynamic in his description of his interaction with a group member, he seems to have remained unaware of how he unconsciously maintains his position of power vis-a-vis the patient by neglecting to inform us of the resolution of this conflict between them. The patient is thereby rendered invisible as is his co-therapist whose voice in this account is conspicuous by its absence. If Mann's reductionist focus on Oedipal issues is correct, then why do women not account for a significant proportion of abusers?

Developing a New NHS Psychotherapy Service and Training Scheme in the Provinces

Mark Aveline

Mark Aveline

St Ann's House, 114 Thorneywood Mount, Nottingham NG3 2PZ

Mark Aveline  

Introduction

The early 1970's saw the beginning of a major investment by the National Health Service in specialist psychotherapy which continues to this day. The expansion was marked by a document from the Royal College of Psychiatrists (1975) which recommended staffing norms for psychotherapy services (now nationally half achieved) and the formal recognition of the medical speciality by the DHSS in 1978. Much of the expansion has taken place in the provinces; its local form has been powerfully influenced by the conceptual affiliations of the new consultants, the presence or absence of established services in the private sector and the relative affluence of the local Health Authority. Generally, the new services have been able to set their own norms and establish innovative patterns of training and staffing. This paper documents what has been achieved in the southern half of one provincial Health Region. In addition, some of the guiding principles, problems and present solutions are presented.

Nottingham Then and Now, 1974 and 1989

The Nottingham NHS service was initiated in 1974 with my appointment. For five years I was the only appointed consultant medical psychotherapist in the Trent Region. Now there are companion units in Leicester (Chris Whyte 1979), Derby (Nassol Constantopoulis 1980-85, David Smith 1985) and Lincoln (Geoff Fisk 1985); a second consultant (Patricia Slack) was appointed in Nottingham in 1987. The Nottingham Psychotherapy Unit has nine full-time and five part-time members of staff drawn from all the mental health care professions and each working as a psychotherapist. It has the accolade of having a fully accredited senior registrarship in psychotherapy, provides a wide range of trainings and clinical services and contributes to the three year plus certifcated South Trent Training in Dynamic Psychotherapy for career psychotherapists that is collaboratively provided by the four units. A consultant in behavioural psychotherapy (Alan King) was appointed in 1981 in Leicester.

A Note on ‘Core Professions’

David Black

David Black

30 Cholmley Gardens, London, NW6 1AG

David Black  

Anyone interested in the development of psychotherapy in the UK must be grateful to Jonathan Pedder for his excellent summary of the recent history and current situation in Courses in Psychotherapy: Evolution and Current Trends (1989). It is splendidly lucid and informative.

I should like, however, to pick out one theme from his paper which I think needs very careful attention. It is the suggestion that ‘entry to the practice and profession of psychotherapy should be via the core professions’. By core professions he means: ‘obviously’ medicine, clinical psychology and social work; apparently less obviously, ‘nursing, occupational therapy, educational backgrounds and so forth’.

This suggestion, he says, ‘I first thought rather conservative but am coming round to think is perhaps right’.

As a first point, let me comment on the word conservative. The reality is that the great majority of the existing psychotherapy trainings have no tradition of regarding medicine, etc, as ‘core professions’ in the sense that there is any necessity to enter the training by way of them. Even Dr Pedder's own organisation, the British Psychoanalytical Society, accepts people from other backgrounds quite readily, and I am not aware that they are regarded in any way as less equipped, having done the training, than the medics and others. Of all the trainings, the only ones whose tradition would be ‘conserved’ by this (in fact) radical innovation would be the adult training of the Tavistock Clinic, certainly an excellent body but unique because of its special relation with the NHS, and perhaps some of the university diploma courses.

Dyne and Figlio (1989), responding on behalf of the ‘independents’, make a second important point: that many excellent therapists come to training in middle life and without such backgrounds. It would be pointless and counter-productive to require them to do massive preliminary trainings of such limited relevance to their mature goals.

Use and Abuse in Psychotherapy

Jackie Gerrard

Jackie Gerrard

39 Lodge Avenue, Elstree, Herts WD6 3NA

Jackie Gerrard  

Oh, don't deceive me; Oh never leave me!

How could you use a poor maiden so?

(Anon. Oxford Song Book)

In this paper I propose to look at the concepts of ‘use’ and ‘abuse’ with reference to the work of Alice Miller and also of Winnicott, and link these ideas with some of my own recent clinical work.

In the above ditty the word ‘use’ has, in essence, the meaning abuse. Don't deceive me (by abusing my trust) or leave me (abandon me) - two significant facets in a situation of abuse, be it child or adult, sexual or non-sexual. I should like to add another feature to the situation of abuse, which perhaps is implied - that of actual, or feared, humiliation.

In her recent work Alice Miller vehemently takes up ideas of abuse of children by their parents. Abuse can come in many forms. It can cover the whole gamut from a lack of respect and non-mirroring, to shaming and humiliating, and to sexual abuse. She has radically revised her thoughts on Freud's drive theory as an explanation of human behaviour and returned to his original trauma theory. She is distressed by what she has called ‘poisonous pedagogy’ in much of today's analytic theory with its adherence to the drive theory and the Oedipus complex. Dr Miller is constantly looking for the patient's story - for what actually happened to that particular patient as an infant and young child. She states ‘in terms of the drive theory parents do not actually abuse their children in order to fulfill their own needs but children supposedly fantasize this abuse, repressing their own aggressive and sexual desires (‘instinctual drives’) and experiencing these desires - through the mechanism of projection - as being directed against them from the outside’ (Miller 1985, p. 4). She is convinced that, if she can understand a person's suffering as a child, she then has the key to understanding a person's entire later life. ‘. … I gained emotional insight into the predicament of the totally dependent child who must repress his trauma if there is no sympathetic and supportive person he can talk to. On the other hand I became increasingly aware of the power adults wield over children’ (p. 6). She says that she concluded that sexual and other disturbances, especially those of a narcissistic nature, are more easily understood when their origins are understood. The helpless child has reacted to the way insecure adults use their power over him. However, she says, ‘since psychoanalytic drive theory encourages the patient's tendency to deny his trauma and blame himself, it is more likely to conceal than to reveal the sexual and narcissistic abuse the patient experienced as a child’ (p. 7). Analysts who work only with the idea that everything that happens to a child is due to his drive conflicts can produce a patient who will end up blaming himself without understanding why he is as he is.

Rational Emotive Therapy

Liam Clarke

Liam Clarke

11 Battle Crescent, Hailsham, East Sussex BN27 IEN

Liam Clarke  

My first exposure to Rational Emotive Therapy (RET) was a demonstration given by Dr W Dryden. It so shocked me that I snatched for my rusty nibbed pen and wrote a skit -most of which forms the tail-end of this piece. In any event I was psychologically set for Dryden's performance in that I had come to believe, generally, that people are much too ‘large’ and complicated (and defended) for ‘modern’ psychotherapies to comprehend and this seemed to be at odds with the ambitious claims of some of these groups. Dr Dryden's (simulated) therapeutic session merely confirmed most of my fears.

Clare (1982) had written cogently about some of these new therapist groups, their idiosyncracies as well as their suspicious commonalities: such that many stem from a disenchantment with psychoanalytic theory and, especially, practice. A charismatic leader comes quickly to the fore often to describe an ‘awakening’ or ‘discovery’ experience which points to a new and enlightened way: Primal Therapy is especially noteworthy here. An institute will be quickly established (with offshoots) plus a journal and training courses of varying length and depth. But above all, the book will be written and, whatever its complexities, these will be conveniently ignored, or modulated, so as to provide a simplified model whose simplicity is suggestive of Truth; the work of Eric Berne is a good example of this. There is a lack of humility about these ‘secular priests’ (North 1972) with their proud and insular claims to dampen human misery.

These issues of insularity, exclusivity and wild assumptions re-emerged when Dryden (1986) questioned the possession of the title ‘British Journal of Psychotherapy’ by a cartel of psychoanalytic groups, stating that this journal represented a branch or type of therapy only. In my view he was making a fair point. Not only are almost all the articles psychoanalytic in nature and content, but there is also a perceptible drift towards the esoteric and (somewhat) distant in a growing number of them. Dryden was invited to write for the journal but, as far as I know, failed to respond. Yet it is easy to witness the burgeoning ‘publication space’ which RET occupies elsewhere; Dr Dryden is extraordinarily prolific in his writing and editing and has shared book publication space (separate chapters usually) on several occasions. It is regrettable that a more substantial contribution was not made by him as a formative part of the (missing) dialectic which should be part of an analytically focused journal. It seemed as if the problem might be one of territory, restrictive practice and a debate about professional ascendancy.

Commentary by a Lancian Psychoanalyst

Bernard Burgoyne

Bernard Burgoyne

Bernard Burgoyne  

Listening to this young woman talk about her sexual life brings one up against questions of knowledge and truth. The form in which one chooses to listen may be dictated by the main concepts of an analytical theory and, if this is a dominant factor of the analytical work, the work suffers. Avoiding distortive intrusions into the speech of the patient is held by most therapists to be the aim directing their choice of interpretation and intervention; upholding a conceptual system which guides the direction of the treatment is much less often recognised as failing to achieve this aim. Comments such as ‘she felt very regressed’ and the interpretation ‘I feel that being a nurse helps in a way to repair the damage’ are examples of such intrusions; in this case the therapist was clearly able to produce an environment in which the patient could produce significant material - yet, sometimes the patient is not listened to and sometimes what she says is not analysed.

At the beginning of the first of the two sessions, Helen presents some object-relations that bear closer investigation. She describes the visit to her flat when her father gave her some support ('her father had helped her to put up some shelves'), and when her mother had left them to get on with this while she did something quite separate. Frequently Helen will describe a situation of her mother leaving her, and here is one state of affairs that can be brought about by that: the daughter-father pair are close to each other while the mother is quite separate from them. Helen's relation to the father is under-analysed by the therapist's interventions; despite having an important position in Helen's presenting symptoms - finding herself in a daughter/father relation with boyfriends - the father is fairly absent from the analytical work presented here. Helen repeatedly presents herself as betrayed by the mother. Who is betrayed? The daughter, or the couple of the daughter and father? It is the mother leaving the girl with the father, as in the flat, that would constitute a betrayal if the aim of the young woman were to constitute a three-person relationship - with herself in the position of being able to control and barter her father's favours. In this question of betrayal, she says of her mother, ‘she cheats’. Now, of course, it is the father who cheats. What remains an open question in this is to what extent the daughter is complicit.

Marco Chiesa  

The terms projection and projective identification have been the object of controversy and different authors assign them different meanings (Crisp 1986). In this paper we shall refer to projective identification as a primitive unconscious fantasy which involves the expulsion of split off parts of the self and of internal objects into an external object (Klein 1946, 1955). This process leads to a fusion of the projected parts of the self with the external object, hence the identification of the former with the latter. As a consequence of projective processes the ego becomes impoverished and more fragile and fear of retaliation from the object is established, leading to the constant need to gain control over it. One most important feature of projective identification is the experience induced in the recipient of the projection of feeling intruded upon; he is being pressurised to feel and behave in a way congruent with the feelings that have been projected into him: the recipient feels possessed by, controlled and identified with the projected material (Ogden 1979). The projector never loses touch with the ridden parts of the self and maintains an empathic rapport with the external object. Projective identification not only serves the function as a defence mechanism of the primitive self (Segal 1982), but can also be considered as an attempt to communicate unbearable states of mind, through forcibly allowing the external object to experience them following their expulsion into the object. If these thoughts and feelings can be contained and ‘psychologically processed’ (Bion 1962) by the recipient, they can subsequently be reintrojected in a more tolerable form and become more meaningful.

In the mother-baby interaction or within a therapeutic relationship this reinternalisation of metabolised projected parts of the self can be responsible for the process of psychological growth. Simple projection can be described as the defence mechanism of externalisation which is involved in the first phase of projective identification. It is questionable that projection can occur without a certain degree of projective identification taking place and what is called simple projection is, in fact, a mild form of projective identification (Bott-Spillius 1983).

The response that we got to the July newsletter was very helpful to the Council, giving us back the feeling of being in communication with our members. We have a serious and unsolvable problem as giving out enough information takes up a lot of paper. If we used less paper our discussions would take place half-blind. The ideas as well as the proposals from the various sub-committees that we have created to do the essential work must be circulated so their work is not duplicated. In the days of the Rugby Psychotherapy Conference I was in touch with everything that was going on, and was a participant in all the discussions. Since our inaugural meeting one year ago that has not been possible as our structure is now developing and more people are involved in the day to day work. The result is a recommendation from Council that we create a new section at our AGM.

This healthy development is essential if we are to grasp our opportunities and get away from relying on any single person. It is important for us to move towards being able to rely on a group that is large enough to keep pushing the work of Conference forward. The difficulty that we inevitably run into is that we come up against the problems of our structure. Whatever structures we evolve as we go along, we will never find any perfect solution and we will always be working with compromises that will have to be altered as the balance of our needs alters over time. Editorial

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood

Bob Hinshelwood  

Repertory grids have been around for a long time, and have been used in a number of research areas in psychology and psychotherapy. They form a method for mapping the systems of meaning used by a human mind, and with which each individual gives himself a structure for thinking about his experience. And it is a method quite remote from psychodynamic concepts.

Unfortunately few psychotherapists know much about the method; and that is because it is to do with the intense mathematical concentration which is required to comprehend the method. And most of us psychotherapists are mathematically slack, one reason we are psychotherapists rather than ‘proper’ scientists. However it seemed worth drawing to the attention of the readers of the Journal the papers we publish in this issue by Ray Brown and Marco Chiesa. Projective identification has also been around for a long time and often seems to have an equally bemused reception. The realisation that it can be tracked down by a research technique and measured with numbers is elegantly demonstrated in the second of these papers. The first is, in contrast, an attempt to provide an introductory overview of this psychological theory that gives rise to the versatile research technique of repertory grids.

David Alexander and John Eagles, in a prospective study, look at much simpler numbers when they investigate clinical, demographic and other variables that affect the chances of receiving psychotherapy of all kinds. As they say, these interesting observations need to be extended to the quality of outcome of the treatments that patients are guided towards. An attempt to look at outcome criteria, and in relation to certain variables at intake, is reported by Cecilia Clementel-Jones, David Malan and Tom Trauer. The psychotherapy was of course wholly psychoanalytic in orientation, but it demonstrated that one of the most important factors in outcome was the length of time in treatment; at least 60 sessions, say a year and a half, before significant improvement is clearly demonstrable. Many generalisations about outcome are from studies of briefer forms of treatment, and these seem therefore be be invalid.

[[RunningHead]]

An Introduction to Repertory Grid Theory and Technique

Ray Brown and Marco Chiesa

Marco Chiesa

Newport, Isle of Wight

Fulham Palace Road, London

Marco Chiesa  

This article is to introduce the reader to repertory grid theory and technique, and to describe some applications of the technique to psychotherapy research. The research potential of the double dyad grid, a development from the repertory grid, will also be discussed.

The late George Kelly, an American psychologist and engineer, drew together a philosophical background, a theory of human personality, a therapeutic approach and a research methodology in the two volumes of The Psychology of Personal Constructs (1955). His style is ‘homespun’, gentle and full of humour in places. Yet his endeavour was serious - to develop an internally coherent theory of human personality. Repertory grid theory and technique have their roots in Kelly's publication. Since 1955 there have been many reviews of, and developments in, Kelly's work. The applications of repertory grid techniques have diversified. The technique is extremely flexible and has been applied in very different research and clinical settings. Grid studies have been carried out in social anthropology (Orley 1976) to investigate Ganda mythology, in the area of architectural and environmental design (Honikman 1976, Stringer 1974), in assessing training programmes (Lipshitz 1974, Ryle & Breen 1974), and in the study of cognitive structure and complexity (Bieri 1955, Epting 1972, Honess 1976). In this article only some of those developments obviously relevant to psychotherapy will be discussed. In formulating his theory of personality, Kelly used a philosophy of ‘constructive alternativism’;. ‘Constructive alternativism falls within that area of epistemology which is sometimes called gnosiology - the systematic analysis of the conceptions employed by ordinary and scientific thought in exploring the world’. Kelly takes an exploration of the ‘theory of theories’ as his starting point for the development of the theory of personal constructs. Events are open to an infinite number of theoretical constructions, the number only limited by the resources of ingenuity. Kelly assumed that ‘all of our present interpretations of the universe are subject to revision or replacement’. Any theory is an invented abstraction from the observations of the perceived patterns of events and is an invention which, while providing a framework, reflexly constrains thought (Kelly 1969, p. 94)

Commentary by a Jungian Annalyst

John Miller

John Miller

John Miller  

A major problem I encounter at the outset of writing a commentary on these two sessions is trying to decide at what level the therapist is working.

477

If what is being attempted is what might loosely be called supportive therapy - trying to enable the patient to feel better about herself without trying to dig too deep, then I have a picture of a sensitive therapist doing a good job. If, on the other hand, what is being attempted is work of analytical depth, I confess I feel less sure of what is being achieved in the two sessions presented.

It looks as if the patient may be someone with quite deep-rooted problems of dependency which are probably related to a severe identity problem. The presenting problem of the dependent relationship with the boyfriend sounds like the symbiotic merging so commonly found where the early bond with the mother was not properly established. Possibly, as an effect of the two miscarriages, the mother was depressed and saw the patient as if she were dead or, in some other way, could not see her as a person in her own right.

To add insult to injury, the poor girl had to suffer early hospitalisations and surgery with further interference of the mother-infant relationship.

A very tough start to life and one which has clearly left its scars. However, this is only one side of things - the external side or what is somewhat misleadingly referred to as the historical background.

But the central issue of analytical work is how the patient has responded to these experiences. What makes up her inner world to which these childhood experiences are only some of the contributory factors? Jung wrote in 1934: ‘The true reason for neurosis lies in the present … it is fed and as it were new-made every day. And it is only in the today, not in our yesterdays, that the neurosis can be “cured”’ (p. 171).

One of the main ways of doing this is working with the transference, which I understand to mean taking all the communications of the patient, whatever their conscious intentions, as being likely to reflect what is unconsciously going on in the transference.

The Fallacy of the ‘Core Profession’

John Rowan

John Rowan

John Rowan  

One of the most insidious fallacies about psychotherapy is that it is based on certain ‘core professions’, and that therefore people should qualify in one of these professions before they can receive further training as psychotherapists.

The three professions usually mentioned in this context are psychology, medicine and social work. It seems to me that there are serious objections to all of them. Medicine trains people to treat the person like a complicated machine, and social work is too closely tied in with issues of social control. But psychology is the one with which I am most familiar, so I will leave it to others to make the corresponding arguments in those areas.

There is of course a certain superficial neatness about the idea of a core profession. If it could be established that there was a particularly suitable preparation offered by an existing profession (or three), this might overcome the obvious objection that such an approach is extremely narrow.

Let us therefore look closely at the preparation given by psychology as taught in existing degree courses at prestigious universities.

The first thing we notice about academic psychology is that it aspires to scientific objectivity. It was a triumph of the British Psychological Association that psychology was in recent years admitted to the pantheon of true sciences in the international community of scientists.

Now the whole point of scientific objectivity, as taught in academia, is that it enables the scientist to stand well back from the phenomena being studied, and not allow subjectivity to spoil the work. The apotheosis of this approach is the controlled experiment where we know what the result means because we have strict control over all the elements involved.

All other methods of studying phenomena are regarded as less valuable than this. Only the controlled experiment gives genuine knowledge because it is only the controlled experiment which eliminates alternative explanations of the phenomenon being studied.

I want to thank Joan Schachter for the thoughts she expressed in her review of Christopher Bollas's Forces of Destiny in this Journal, (6(3)). By the way she pulled together what she saw as the central points I had one of those celebratory ‘AHA’ experiences. Now I'd like to comment on it. It is the idea of a free act in an experience of encounter. I am a newly qualified analytic psychotherapist who often feels like a car without a proper make. I do not sometimes know who to belong to, which school, which ‘mast’ do I nail my heart to? I know certainly that two of my ‘of the essence’ papers from analytic practice are the two that Schachter referred to. When I first read Symington's and Coltart's papers they were to me like sweet smells of fresh air, sunshine on my shoulder, etc. I wondered why they were not required reading in training. They describe free acts which can be understood and cherished as just that. It is confusing to me that often such acts are labelled ‘acting out’. The label turns a form of human intimacy into a destructive ‘you need more analysis’ deed. (In fact I wonder if people reading this commentary will think the same of me!) I am not saying that there is not such a thing as ‘acting out’. And I realise that this topic which I am touching on is complex and needs very careful untangling but I am at the beginning. It seems to me that all too frequently basic human gestures are too easily lumped into the category of ‘acting out’. Such sensitive spontaneous acts of analytic practice seem to be so suspect. For me what is suspect is a too rigid analytic stance. Could one ask if the stance could be an ‘acting out’? A way of control, of keeping everything within a talking framework; is it out of an unspoken ‘keeping in’ with The Elders, The True Ones, The Heritage? In the presence of such illustrious Ones I wonder if there is room to play, if there is room to find, to be aware of human interactions which are closer to realms of performance, of gesture, of sound, of the nonverbal. I would ask readers, the editor, writers, for some feedback on this topic of the boundaries around ‘acting out’, gesture, acts of play, acts of sensitivity within the analytic framework … other papers, articles, books -material for a closer look into the matter.

Crises of the Self: Further Essays on Psychoanalysis and Politics edited by Barry Richards. Published by Free Association Books, London, 1989; 278 pages, £12.95 paperback.

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon

Paul Gordon  

The further that psychoanalytic thought moves away from the analytic situation the more tenuous become its possible insights. From Freud onwards, the history of psychoanalysis is littered with social and political speculation that is either banal or spurious. It is to the merit of most of the contributors to this book - as it is to the Free Associations project as a whole - that they manage to look at a wide range of political matters with the benefits of psychoanalysis without falling into these traps.

To call something a crisis these days is, as editor Barry Richards remarks in his introduction, a very ordinary description, usually heralding some cliched analysis. And yet, as Richards maintains rightly, crises there are, even if their nature is longterm, perhaps even perpetual. And with all such crises - be they of political beliefs, gender or racial identity or existence itself - the external social world is not an inert backcloth but an active constituent.

I am not convinced that everything in this book relates to a ‘crisis’ in any meaningful sense and a more accurate title might have been found, but that is a minor point. It is certainly undeniable that all the papers respond in some way to problems of contemporary experience, usually by means of Kleinian or object relations theory. These include the collapse of political certainties (Paul Hoggett), culture (Robert Young, touching and amusing, on transitional phenomena; Jed Sekoff on the ‘minddoctor film’ - but why no mention of one of the best and most serious attempts in this genre, Ken McMullen's Zina?), gender and sexual identity (Amal Treacher on advice in women's magazines; Marie Maguire on gendered disorders), racial identity (Stephen Frosh, Philip Cohen and Valerie Sinason) and survival itself (Jane Temperley on the nuclear threat).

Implicit in much of the book is a welcome argument against the excesses of postmodernism, in particular the celebration of fragmentation. Psychoanalysis, as Barry Richards shows in his fascinating account of its urban origins, was a response to the experience of modern urbanism. Its emergence in Vienna and subsequent development in London, Berlin and New York were due, not just to the existence of a potential market and a degree of professional specialisation, but also to the sense of fragmentation experienced by the inhabitants of the great modern cities. While arguing for psychoanalysis' reparative abilities, Richards concludes that psychoanalysis also reminds us that a certain ‘substrate of chaos and terror’ must remain. In similar vein, Paul Hoggett suggests that while we may have to live in a ‘culture of uncertainty’, a world ‘in which all previous answers have ceased to serve’, this does not mean lapsing into the hatred and despair of those who celebrate the end of thought or the accommodation of cynicism. We can indeed only gasp when the ‘ultimate nightmare of psychosis’ becomes ‘high fashion’ for others, presumably those who have escaped the nightmare itself only to celebrate it in others.

The Philadelphia Association is probably best known through R D Laing, one of its founders, and its work in providing households for people in severe mental distress, the most famous (or infamous) being Kingsley Hall in London's East End. This, however, is just a small part of this ‘Philadelphia story’ for, since its formation in 1964, the Association has also developed its own approach to psychoanalytic psychotherapy - reflected in this book of papers by Association members - and its own psychotherapy training programme which has existed since 1969.

A chapter in this book outlines, frankly it seems, the history of the Association. While acknowledging the organisation's debt to Laing, it makes it clear that Laing's role was only part of its development. Not only did many others play key roles, people like David Cooper, Aaron Esterson and Hugh Crawford, but Laing's involvement brought its own problems. The other side of the coin of his creativity was a lack of responsibility and sustained interest. That and Laing's increasing flirtation with humanistic psychology, including mass ‘rebirthings’ at the Inn on the Park on a Sunday afternoon, meant an inevitable parting of the ways.

Beyond such a history, one immediately encounters difficulties in trying to define or explain the Philadelphia Association. This is a point made by Chris Oakley on the first page of the book when he writes, ‘one comes up against a persistent indirectness. What unfolds is a lattice-work of complicated intersections’. One strand in this lattice is a highly critical view of orthodox psychoanalysis.

International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 71, Part 1, 1990

The Possibility of Human Freedom and its Transmission (with Particular Reference to the Thought of Bion) Neville Symington

Neville Symington

In this paper I examine where Bion's theory of freedom fits within the traditional philosophical debate. I claim that the notion of freedom is the organizing centre of Bion's thought and that the traditional debate has focused with too great a concentration upon the will. I propose that underlying the workings of the will there is a fundamental substratum. This is governed either by the reaction model or by the response model. Freedom is coextensive with the latter mode of functioning but not with the former. The traditional debate needs to take this layer of personality functioning into account.



International Journal of Psycho-Analysis, Volume 71, Part 1, 1990

Beyond Semantics: A Clinical and Theoretical Study of Isolation

Bjorn Killingmo

Theories of Freud, Piaget, Fonagy and Kristeva have been drawn on to argue that the concept of isolation should not be restricted to a delimited defence mechanism associated with obsessional/compulsive neurosis, as is the usual psychoanalytic conception. From a semiological point of view isolation may be seen as a disturbance of the relationship between signifier and the signified embracing affective communication ranging from the most primitive bodily expression via sound and intonation to a semantic level where affects are expressed through the content of words and ideas. As affects isolated on a pre-verbal level are deprived of expression on a semantic-symbolic level, they are not likely to be modified by content of interpretations alone. They can only be fully activated and brought into therapeutic dialogue through the quality of the speech sound of the analyst.
