Clinical Commentary XI

[This section is a regular feature. A short piece of clinical material from an actual session is presented with a brief introduction about the case. The material has been sent ‘blind’ to three people who represent different psychotherapeutic schools of thought. They have been asked to comment on the material and the approach of the therapist in the session. The intention is to put these commentaries on the same material side by side for comparison of the different approaches and to facilitate the understanding of alternative terminologies and modes of practice - Ed]

The therapist writes:

The History

F is a six-year-old boy, younger son by many years of wealthy business parents. He was left in the care of frequently changing nannies and au pairs from five days of age. His mother had been worried about him since she was told during pregnancy that he had a small head. F had been intensively investigated and no physical handicap had been found. F was referred by the parents for exposing himself and spitting at home and at school, which resulted in difficulties in finding education for him. The parents were worried that he would not be able to go into the family business.

F was assessed for psychotherapy and was offered four times weekly therapy. The session presented took place nine months into the therapy, on a Monday, after a missed Friday. Unknown to the therapist F's latest nanny had just left.

The Session

F came ten minutes early with Don, a new escort - a gentle older man. He encouraged F to come when F ignored me. ‘Look, I've got short sleeves.’ F stroked his arms and approached me with both hands as if to touch me.

By the lifts F looks at Don and then at me, saying ‘Mother-Fucker, shit’, etc. He looks back at Don as if to demonstrate his abusive relationship with me. He smiles to Don as he goes on swearing at me and Don tells him gently to stop. He is still smiling as he goes into the room in the wrong direction and smiles in a lively way as I point him the right way to the room.

James Astor

James Astor

James Astor  

My understanding of this session derives from the impact of the weekend break, in the context of the broken intimacy between mother and baby. I experienced F as a baby whose relationship to the breast had been interrupted, a baby of extraordinary resilience and determination fighting for exclusive possession of his therapist mother. The first part of the session is concerned with the way he slips into tyrannical behaviour and gives into this part of himself, severely taxing his therapist in the enactment of his tyranny. The change occurs in her containment of his tantrum and the way she was able skilfully to help F be safely in touch for a short while with his depressive feelings.

The session begins with F smiling, pleased to see his therapist but struggling against the abusive little tyrant in him who fills the inside of the therapist mummy with shit over the three-day break. He is a little boy with a short sleeve penis, wondering if mummy therapist will like him and want to touch him as much as he imagines she has enjoyed touching her long-sleeved daddy-husband over the weekend. (This refers to his weekend masturbatory attacks on the parents' intercourse.) Just seeing the therapist seems to have disorientated him (going in the wrong direction to the room) as if through his eyes he is going into a state of projective identification with the inside of her body which he later tells us is a big mess. He turns out the cupboard in a sadistic and physically violent manner. What has changed inside mummy over the weekend? Is there any evidence of mummy therapist's inside having been visited by a big Daddy, the mother fucker inside the mummy which he refers to at the beginning of the session? He concludes his attack on the inside of his therapist-mummy's body with the statement that it is a ‘big mess today’.

While this statement is triumphant in tone (referring to the job he has done to reassert an imaginary control over the inside of mummy) there is buried in this a poignancy in his acknowledgement that the weekend has internally been awful for him; a good mummy therapist has been filled in his mind with angry shit.

The Arbours, 20 + Years

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke  

For the Arbours the past five years have seen a period of consolidation as well as careful expansion of our activities. Our long-stay communities are now registered as hostels, which means our basic facilities are reasonably secure and that we are able to accept people as residents regardless of means.

During this time an important event that brought together the residents of the communities and Crisis Centre was an exhibition of Arbours Art that took place at the Smith Gallery in Covent Garden last autumn. This was the culmination of several years of effort by the residents and Julia Saltiel, the Arbours art therapist. But perhaps ‘art therapy’ connotes something too precise and limiting. The work was not done as therapy per se but as a creative development in the lives of everyone involved. The exhibition included paintings, drawings, sculpture, fashion and photography, much done to the highest standards.

At the Crisis Centre we have completed an attic extension, which has allowed us to open a sixth guest bedroom and a second consultation room. I would like to extend special thanks to the Planned Environment Therapy Trust for financial help with this project. We have also been refining our capacity to support the many chaotic and severely damaged individuals and families who are referred to us by reducing the turnover of the key helpers at the Centre. Towards this end we are now able to accept suitable candidates at any time by creating the post of sponsored applicant. Having been accepted as a sponsored applicant, the individual joins our training programme, begins to be involved with the work of the Centre and receives a small bursary. Then when an opening is available he or she can move into the Centre and avoid the long process of familiarisation that would otherwise be necessary.

Similarly our training programme is doing well. We have an increasing number of candidates and have continued to expand our links with other training organisations. I think that it is well worth emphasising that a special feature of our programme is the fact that our trainees have a unique opportunity for direct clinical experience by working at our Communities and Crisis Centre.

International Pact (Parents and Children Together) for Peaceful Negotiations by the United Nations

Joan Raphael-Leff

Joan Raphael-Leff

Joan Raphael-Leff  

As health-care professionals, I believe we have a duty to speak out against a policy which assumes war to be a viable solution to political conflict. I find myself in the unusual position of speaking for many hundreds of people who, over the past months since I began writing letters and articles in newspapers here and abroad, have responded by signing a pact supporting the United Nations in upholding peaceful negotiations rather than military efforts in the Gulf.

Inevitably, I've drawn flack accusing me of political naivete. My answer is that it is naive to believe modern war can be brief or successful. Those of us like myself, who have been to war know that unlike playground or fantasy battles, effects persist long beyond military action. Ordinary people are killed, mourned, maimed or displaced and every individual participant and world witness is irreversibly changed for the worse. Furthermore, in the present climate, war which arose to corner a desperate Saddam Hussein, would inevitably result in vast destruction of life and devastation of regions far beyond the local Persian Gulf.

In opposing war we can unite around our basic common denominator- that of being parents and/or children of parents. Acknowledgement that we all share similar early experiences and the same basic needs (for reciprocal recognition, creature comforts and personal space) can form a bridge across political, ethnic, religious and geographical divides. Indeed, supporters of PACT for peaceful negotiations have come from places as diverse in ideology as England, Sweden, Germany and Israel.

Force is never the only option and no single leader is infallible. We must exercise our human capacity to talk - use thought and words rather than resorting to action, and have a say in our fate rather than complying in being passive bystanders. I believe our hope for peace lies politically in reenforcing the UN as an international government in which we all have representative and consultant status, and as individuals, caring enough to become a worldwide guardian movement beyond this immediate crisis.

Schizogenesis

Stuart Cox

Stuart Cox

Stuart Cox  

Dear Sir

I read the article by Robin Royston in the British Journal of Psychotherapy, Vol. 6(1) with interest and excitement.

The author reviews some of the relevant research in the field of the genetics of schizophrenia but did not mention one fact that plagues exponents of a strictly biological causation of this illness. This fact is that the psychotic illnesses do not ‘breed true’. That is to say, schizophrenic patients have an increased chance that their children (and other first degree relatives) will also have schizophrenia; but there is also an increased risk of other psychotic illnesses such as psychotic depression and manicdepressive psychosis as well. Thus it seems as if it is the capacity to be psychotic rather than the particular form of the illness that seems to be inherited.

The author reviews Jung's theories of psychosis: that psychotic material forces itself into consciousness, either because of its own particular power, or because consciousness is too weak to hold it back. Another hypothesis, which has advantages that I shall go on to discuss, is that there exists in normal people a ‘filtering mechanism’, not activated whilst dreaming, or deactivated in toxic organic states, that is weakened or absent in those people who develop psychotic illness. This filter would roughly correspond to the horizontal dotted line in Robin Royston's diagram. It would not matter whether the filter had its origin in the biochemical or structural nature of the brain for the validity of this idea.

The author then turns his attention to the work of Melanie Klein. If it was a defective filtering mechanism that was responsible for the development of psychotic illness, then the actual form taken in an individual patient might depend upon the stage that patient reached in early development before the disruption to the normal process of progression from the paranoid-schizoid to the depressive position occurred. Early disruption might lead to schizophrenia, and at a later stage to psychotic depression.

Know What I Mean: An Exploration into Knowing What is Meant

Fiona Gardner

Fiona Gardner

8 St Saviour's Terrace, Larkhall, Bath, Avon BA1 6RL

Fiona Gardner  

Introduction

This study was prompted by the frequent use of the expression ‘know what I mean’ by a patient, J. The meaning of the expression changed over three years of weekly sessions. Initially it felt like an order to know and a demand that the patient brought to the treatment. Over time the command changed to a question offering more space between the patient and myself. As the space enlarged sufficiently for the patient to recognise myself as other, she prefixed the question ‘do you know what I mean?’. After three years the patient had stopped using the expression, and by then we were both perhaps able to accept that I did not always know what she meant, but that the therapy offered the opportunity to explore the meaning together.

The statement reflected the patient's lonely and misunderstood experiences as a child and adolescent, but the search for ‘knowing the meaning’ brought forward complex issues both about the work with the patient and about my acceptance of becoming and being a psychotherapist.

The definition of ‘knowing’ includes: recognition; having personal experience of, being aware of, and having, the technical expertise. The definition of ‘meaning’ includes: having in mind; intending to convey and signify. At its most superficial, ‘know what I mean’ is an almost meaningless reflex colloquialism. In the therapeutic setting the phrase has a superficial level - the therapist can be aware of what the patient is intending to convey. At a deeper level recognition of what the patient has in mind and is signifying is much harder. When commanded to understand, the therapist can only reflect back her/his recognition of the patient's need to be understood and, as the words shift, the therapist can work with the patient in the transference to reveal the deeper significance.

Knowing what is meant carries with it its counterpart, not knowing what is meant. In turn the conscious meaning also has its counterpart: the unconscious meaning, the meaning which is underneath that which is knowingly meant. This underlying meaning may only gradually emerge through the transference relationship. Lacan (1979) refers to the being of the subject as ‘that which is beneath the meaning’, and points out the dilemma in holding the two aspects for, in focusing on one alone, the other will disappear. If we choose to focus only on the unconscious, the being, then, as Lacan explains, the subject disappears and only non-meaning is left. If we only see the meaning the unconscious is ignored and the process becomes one-dimensional. The words ‘do you know what I mean’ can become ‘do you understand my unconscious’.

It is quite common nowadays to discover that a large number of adults find that their offspring or their child clients constitute the first instance of their coming close to a child. This may be due to changes in the structure of the family or to modern life in bigger connurbations but, whatever the cause, it is not rare to find professionals with a thorough knowledge of what various schools postulate as the early stages of a child's emotional development, who nevertheless feel baffled and ill-at-ease when they have to deal with a real child. Stern (1985) put forward the notion of the ‘conceptual child’ to describe this construct with which every psychology or biology student is familiar, but which is dramatically different from a real, live child.

For some years now, Infant Observation has been part of the curriculum of several training courses devoted to a psychodynamic approach to the treatment of children and adults. This is a welcome development in that it enables (forces?) students to have a close, intimate contact with real children and parents before they embark on the study of the concepts that aim to explain their characteristics and mutual influences. Furthermore, this exercise leads the student to experience the complexity of the role of observer: particularly when he/she is moving on to learn about transference and counter-transference and the debate about the analyst/therapist as mirror or otherwise, the weekly visits to a family constitute a challenge for him/her to learn how to share without intruding, how to observe without becoming detached, how to acknowledge and show feelings without acting on prejudice.

Clearly, there are many ways of conducting an Infant Observation course and it is unavoidable that each teacher should convey, overtly or covertly, his personal theoretical framework. Indeed, the course unfolds in parallel to the students' exposure to other lecturers so that, beside bringing their own personal professional baggage, the students are also eager to pick up the theories and techniques of their new training. What distinguishes a good course from a bad one is the extent to which the seminar leader insists that the student should stick to his observations and take them as the points of departure for his theoretical formulations - rather than forcing them in a procrustean fashion into the theories taught in his new training.

This paper provides an account of a six-month psychotherapy group for incest survivors in the setting of an all-women centre. It looks at the high level of anxiety expressed by the group members and their struggles with the two women therapists. The paper stresses the attempts to split the co-therapist couple and the importance of resisting this splitting in order to offer protection and containment to the group. It suggests that the experience of having this containment provided by two women therapists challenged their denigration of women/mothers, which in turn affected their ability to stand up to their abusers. The wish to find a way to relate to their own mothers is considered a powerful motivation for members having joined the group. This is seen as an important part of the separation-individuation process which the incest had denied them.

I am impressed by the enormous emotional impact of this session with F. The brief description of his history is extremely painful to read, and aspects of it seem to be brought vividly alive in the session.

While I believe that, theoretically, the therapist and I might be in agreement about the meaning of this little boy's material, there are some points where I disagree with her. I should also like to look at some important technical questions in interpreting to such a vulnerable and fragile child patient. Consideration of technique, however, is a different matter in examining a session after the event, especially somebody else's session! In the heat of the moment, in a therapy room, with a patient like F, a Child Psychotherapist has a very different task from colleagues who work with adults. Examination of the transference, and of one's countertransference, may be hindered while one is avoiding hard missiles, accurately aimed, considering the physical safety of the patient, and contemplating the ‘big mess’ which must later be cleaned up. Literally!

The beginning of the session, in the waiting room, by the lifts and getting to the therapy room, reveals the patient's state of mind and the transference after a longerthan-usual weekend break. F seems to be in projective identification with the kind of man, or father, whose contempt for women and their weekend sexual behaviour shows no pain. He is facing in the wrong direction and may have in mind his absent therapist who is seen as the bad, sexual mother who turns her back on her children. (In the transference the therapist is, in Bion's words, the personification of the bad object, present and persecuting, for the patient, made bad by his aggressive projections and fury/horror at being separated from her.) His identification also seems to include the idea that other men (Don) share this view of weekend-women. Nonetheless there is a hint of something else. F is easily turned in the right direction by the therapist and she describes his walk to the room as lively.

Bela Grunberger's importance as a theorist of narcissism was first made evident to English-speaking audiences with the publication of Narcissism, Psychoanalytic Essays (International Universities Press) in 1979. With the publication of this further series of essays, the potency of Grunberger's critique of narcissism becomes more apparent, as

192

do some of its underlying ideological constraints. Despite the unwieldy literary nature of the book, produced by the repetitive outlining of Grunberger's basic theory in almost every essay, this is a collection of considerable importance. Narcissism has become emblematic of a certain way of being under conditions of modernity; in some instances, as in the work of Christopher Lasch, it has become a characterisation of contemporary consumer society as a whole. In this book, Grunberger offers the most trenchant available psychoanalytic critique of the regressive nature of pure narcissism and thus, both directly and indirectly, demonstrates the dangers of a culture that produces narcissism as a common structure of personality.

Grunberger's book has a number of important threads, including an intriguing analysis of antisemitism, an oppositional stance towards Lacan which nevertheless powerfully employs some Lacanian concepts, and an account of the relationships between ego ideal and super-ego linked closely to the work of Grunberger's collaborator Chasseguet-Smirgel. In this review, however, I am going to focus on the central elements of Grunberger's theory of the origins and nature of narcissism and the sense in which he regards it as a regressive phenomenon. It is this aspect of his work which is most in need of wider dissemination and appraisal.

Grunberger locates the origins of narcissism in the prenatal state of the foetus, which he refers to as ‘prenatal coenesthesis’ - a perfect state of holistic completeness. This state is the source of all the sensations of regressive narcissism, sensations which derive their powerful positive pull from the fact that their actual illusoriness is rooted in an earlier condition in which they were the truth of the subject's existence (p. xii)

Josephine Klein

Josephine Klein

58 Roupell Street, London SE 1 8TB

Josephine Klein  

‘Patients who are not ready for interpretations’. A friend criticised this title on the ground that it implies some unreadiness on the part of the patient, not to be ready for something. As though patients ought to be available for interpretations, as though interpretation is what psychotherapy is about. This is not what I believe. Psychotherapy is therapy: it is about enabling people to explore their processes, conscious and unconscious, so that they can understand better what they are doing in their lives and gain some control over the alternatives which are in principle available to them. We know that it can be helpful, in pursuit of this goal, to interpret to people the unconscious meaning of what they are doing or feeling or thinking. But we also know of people we are not able to help by this means, and therefore a more accurate if clumsier title would have been ‘Patients for whom interpretations are inappropriate’. Or, even more accurately, ‘Patients for whom interpretation of unconscious material is inappropriate’. What I find inappropriate with particular people is for me to bring in aspects of their experience of which they are unconscious, which are ego-alien to them and sound strange to them.

My first example is of someone who could not tolerate what she experienced as my intrusiveness.

I saw ‘Rose’ for more than ten years, from her early twenties onwards. She came twice a week to me individually and once a week to a group I run. She was dreadfully depressed, anxious, and generally unalive, living most of the time in what she described as a grey fog. In the first couple of years I interpreted in the normal way what I thought was happening to her or between us. She seemed to listen to what I said, often agreeing, and we got nowhere much except that she did keep coming. I cannot take much credit for this, for eary in her third year she was able to tell me that she had not exactly come for therapy: she had been sent by an unfortunate alliance of her boyfriend and her mother, who had said she needed it because of her sexual unresponsiveness. I then got some glimpse of how much had been invasive in her life. I also saw the validity of my feeling that I was being kept at bay, but discussing this led nowhere. She mainly talked about current problems and distresses, and I mainly listened, sympathised, occasionally putting forward alternative possibilities. It was to be years before her resentment at my giving advice surfaced in the sessions. However, she put up with it and kept coming.

Jeremy Holmes  

Introduction

In the opening scenes of Evelyn Waugh's novel Scoop, William Boot, nature correspondent of the daily Beast, famous for such lines as ‘Feather-footed through the plashy fen passes the questing vole …’, is summoned from his remote country seat to the metropolis. The newspaper's proprietor, Lord Copper, has been tricked by the brilliantly scheming Mrs Algernon Stitch into appointing Boot war correspondent to the Civil War in the remote country of Ishmaelia. Copper brooks no refusal; every time Boot protests that his speciality is nature, not war, he doubles his salary. Boot goes and eventually returns a hero having, through sheer naïvety and luck, got the story which eluded the sophisticated Fleet Street journalists. But he was the wrong Boot all along. Mrs Stitch's protégé was Courtney Boot, the fashionable novelist.

Memories of this plot came to mind when I read, with excitement and some anxiety, Joan Raphael-Leff's invitation to give this third British Journal of Psychotherapy annual lecture. Had they got the wrong person? What could a rural refugee, only partially assimilated into the mainstream of psychotherapy, have to offer that would be relevant or interesting? But then, like Waugh's readers, I abandoned myself to the oedipal reverie of the changeling, the naïve younger brother who with the help of the good fairy outflanks the corrupt patriarchal order. Tempering this phantasy with reality, I began to think that perhaps there was something to be said for a view from the periphery, a rural worm's-eye view of urban psychotherapy. I reminded myself that Waugh had also made a move from London to the West Country, that Scoop marks the transition from the witty chronicler of the gay young things of the thirties to the more serious concerns of his later novels; that psychotherapy might need, if not a barefoot view, at least a gum-Boot as well as a Gucci.

To continue in this home-spun vein, I sometimes at the start of a psychotherapy session picture it as a tangled skein of wool in need of unravelling. The first task is to find a loose end and to work back from that to the main theme of the session.

The Observed Infant of Attachment Theory

Juliet Hopkins

Juliet Hopkins

Belsize Lane. London NW3

Juliet Hopkins  

Introduction

The infant of attachment theory has been created to explain the behaviour of infants rather than to explain in the free associations of adults on the couch. Consequently few psychotherapists have become attached to it. This would not surprise its originator, John Bowlby, who has recognised our insecure profession's need to cling to established theories and to their parental figures rather than risk exploring new territories. Our clinical work is fraught with anxiety and uncertainty, and we need to rely on familiar theories to sustain us as we work. As clinicians we value the security provided by the familiar but in our role as scientists we must risk exploring the new. Attachment theory is centrally concerned with this in-built polarity between the need for security and the desire for exploration and mastery of the environment, a polarity that is most obvious in toddlers but is with us throughout life.

Why should psychotherapists explore this new territory and familiarise themselves with the attachment infant? One good reason might be a wish not to be left behind. Attachment theory is becoming the chosen language of an increasing number of developmental psychologists and of professional workers in child mental health in both America and Europe. It is, for example, the development within psychoanalysis which is now widely adopted within the World Association for Infant Psychiatry. It has stimulated a significant advance in child development research and its contribution has been widely welcomed by child psychologists (e.g. Sroufe 1986). A further good reason to explore it is the increasing relevance of attachment research for developmental psychopathology and for preventive mental health. The psychoanalysis of adults is unlikely by itself to give us further insights into the infantile origins of pathology. It is likely that more can be learned by relating these insights to observations of parent-child interactions. As Winnicott (1957) wrote, ‘By constantly co-operating, analysts and direct observers may be able to correlate what is deep in analysis with what is early in infant development’.

Petruska Clarkson  

This article distinguishes, theoretically and by means of clinical examples, dreams and kinship metaphors, between five different kinds of psychotherapeutic relationship which may be potentially available for constructive use in psychotherapy. These are: the Working Alliance; the Transferential/Countertransferential Relationship; the Reparative/Developmentally Needed Relationship; the I-You Relationship; and the Transpersonal Relationship. These five modalities can act as an integrative framework for different traditions (or approaches) of psychotherapy notwithstanding apparently irreconcilable schisms or popular stereotypes.

Nina Coltart  

It was very pleasing to me to be asked to give the paper tonight for the celebration of the 20th Anniversary of the Arbours Association. I have been one of their supporters from the beginning, and for ten years I had the privilege of being on their Training Committee. During that time I had a special function which meant that I came to know a large number of them in a very special way. It linked up directly with one of my other interests which had been the building up and running of a consultation practice at home: nearly 30 years ago now, it struck me that there was a gap in the London scene where it seemed that a sort of broker was needed. There were not as many good psychotherapists around then as there are now, but even so there were quite a few, and quite a few analysts who too often were short of patients. On the other hand, when I was still working in the NHS, I not only discovered that it is almost impossible to do good, detailed, long therapy there, but also that there were plenty of potential patients for such therapists and analysts and that many of these patients could get together the price of a couple of sessions a week, simply by deciding that having some therapy might be more important than two or three nights in the pub or a visit to the movies. So I started the consultation practice to try to bring the two together and ‘match’ them if possible, a process I became more interested in as time went by. When I worked for Arbours, all the students to be trained were of course carefully selected by members of the Admission Committee; then they would come and see me for a single long discussion, after which I would place them with an analyst for what is the central feature of their three-year training as therapists, the training analysis which they committed themselves to, three times a week or possibly more, for anything up to eight years. Analysts in training have to do this, too, but have to attend five times a week. In fact, the frequency of sessions is one of the few things that distinguishes full analysis from analytical psychotherapy. From that meeting I took an interest in the various individuals I had met that way, during their trainings, and of course this paid off over the years as they would qualify and start their own practices and I gained a growing pool of good Arbours therapists to whom to refer new patients from the consultation service, who did not need or want full analyses. And I also came to know the senior, pioneering members of Arbours, who were mostly on the Training Committee, very well over a long period and continued to observe the growth of Arbours with great admiration. They built a thorough analytic training for their students, created a low fee clinic for patients, established and nurtured their community houses, ran the Crisis Centre, and earned themselves a unique and respected place on the London therapy scene.

Inclined towards Klein: A Review of R. D. Hinshelwood's ‘A Dictionary of Kleinian Thought’

James Grotstein

James Grotstein

9777 Willshire Blvd, Beverly Hills, CA 90212, USA

James Grotstein  

Hinshelwood's Dictionary, like all dictionaries, attempts to circumscribe and define a particular domain of interest and then specify and individualise the principal component entities in that domain. A dictionary succeeds when the reader can consult it without disappointment as to the entry he/she wishes to look up and when he/she leaves with an unexpected expansion of his/her knowledge. By this and other criteria the Dictionary succeeds admirably.

The work is organised into two main sections, the first, ‘Main Entries’, explicating the thirteen most important and most basic Kleinian ideas and the second, ‘General Entries’, detailing 143 random entries about important but less critical items. Each entry is organised in turn into the item or thought itself, a complete chronology and history of the development of the specific thought, the varied individual components which comprise the thought, a plethora of invaluable cross-references to related concepts detailed in other parts of the work, a comparison, when possible, with equivalent thoughts from other schools and, finally, the relevant bibliography for the item. Finally, he ends the book with an extensive and virtually complete bibliography of the works of Klein and of Kleinian authors in general. One most interesting result of this method of explication is the emergence of a gratifyingly holographic view of Kleinian thought. It is as if each entry is a recapitulation of the whole but from a different perspective each time. What is missing is an index but that lack has been partially compensated for by the dictionary format itself.

The work is characterised by an eminently readable style. Most Kleinian authors, and I include myself among them, seem to write in a recondite jargonistic manner which too often excludes, alienates and/or inspires envy and contempt, let alone evokes non-credibility. This work is a notable exception. Further, the author clearly delineates the differences between concepts which are held in joint tenancy by the classical and Kleinian schools but which are thought of quite differently by each, e.g. transference, countertransference, technique, phantasies versus fantasies, the oedipus complex, etc. When Winston Churchill observed, ‘The United States and Great Britain are two great democracies divided by a common language’, his words could find no more fitting application than to the differences within the similarities between these two schools.

Towards the end of her life Anna Freud was increasingly upset by the various and accumulating attempts to write psychoanalytic history: Roazen, Eduardo Weiss and of course Jeffrey Masson. All her life she had been guardian of the temple for the faithful for this had also been her first testing in the fire of psychoanalytic debate back in the mid-twenties when she felt called upon to sustain an ‘orthodox’ opposition to the form of child analysis that had gradually been developed in Berlin by Melanie Klein, and in London by Nina Searl and others. Elisabeth Young-Bruehl, in this new biography of Anna Freud, has captured remarkably well the lifelong uncertainty that Anna Freud had over her own identity: she was a prolongation of the dying and dead senior Freud, or was she a psychoanalytic adventurer in her own right?

This volume does not make any particular distinctions between counselling and psychotherapy preferring instead to collapse these activities along with other forms of ‘helping profession’ like social work. This is presumably deliberate for in thereby widening the book's appeal the authors are able to argue for the importance of supervision in a wide range of helping modalities and contexts. Hawkins and Shohet quite rightly point out the relative dearth of supervisory texts available and therefore this book may be viewed as an attempt to design a package that fulfills an identifiable niche in the market. The book is well timed for both counselling and psychotherapy, through the respective organs of the BAC and UKSCP, are struggling with the sort of internal housekeeping and public image issues which preoccupy professions that have yet to obtain secure recognition and autonomy. Part of this struggle, at an internal level, involves developing principles of practice on which recognition criteria, like accreditation, can be successfully grafted. One such principle is supervision, increasingly seen as crucial to practice by counsellors as well as psychotherapists. (In terms of the general availability of supervision it has to be said that, at least as far as the provinces and many NHS contexts are concerned, it is a case of stimulating needy appetite without providing the food. However, that is another matter.)

Interestingly, the frontispiece quote is quis custodiet ipsos custodes? translated as ‘who will care and protect the carers?’ Another less humanistic, more literal interpretation has been ‘who guards the guards?’, which perhaps emphasises the gatekeeping function of supervision concerned with professional interests and standards. Certainly supervision of a managerial and agency-based variety, where issues of accountability are complex, places this gatekeeping function at least on a par with a purely personal/professional development model.

Christopher Lucas  

Some features of a series of male genital exhibitionists seen at the Portman Clinic by the author over a seven-year period are described. A brief historical background is provided and important changes in theoretical thinking are noted, in particular the shift in emphasis from explanatory models stressing castration anxiety to a framework in which anxiety and anger in earlier object relationships are seen as of central importance. Exhibiting behaviour may be regarded as a way of attempting to restore damaged self-esteem by an act of sexualised revenge towards a symbolic mother, whilst at the same time challenging but seeking containment from a symbolic father.

The Screening Function of Post-Traumatic Nightmares

Melvin Lansky

Melvin Lansky

1100 Glendon Avenue, Suite 1527, Los Angeles, California 90024.

Melvin Lansky  

I

Nightmares, especially post-traumatic nightmares, have posed major problems for the theory of dreams. If it is presumed that the manifest dream is virtually unmodified representation of the traumatic event - something like a vivid, affect-laden night-time memory - then it would seem that the manifest and latent ‘content’ of the dream are identical, and there is neither dream work nor the representation of unconscious wishes as fulfilled, nor the need for distortion and disguise that accompanies the expression of unconscious wishes. Furthermore, since nightmares are anxiety dreams which wake the sleeper, the function of dreams as guardians of sleep is not in evidence. Affects in dreams are presumably dampened but certainly not amplified (Freud 1900, p. 467). Accordingly, the enormity of affect - which has made the word ‘nightmare’ paradigmatic for overwhelmingly frightful experience in the face of which one is helpless - seems to belie the stimulus modulating function of dreams.

Perhaps the most perplexing feature of the nightmare revolves around the issue of wish fulfilment. If a dream is the disguised expression of an unconscious wish represented as fulfilled, how is one to account for the generation in dream life of an unmodified replay of an experience of sudden and overwhelming trauma? The dream, in recreating the terrifying experience, seems to act in ways utterly different from that in which stimuli or wishes are represented as fulfilled by the consummatory act of hallucination that we call dreaming.

These issues, of course, have a prominent place in the history of psychoanalysis. Writing of anxiety dreams, Freud (1900) was careful to demonstrate that such dreams were only apparent contradictions of the theory of wish fulfilment. The anxiety, he took great pains to point out, belonged not to the manifest dream scene which appeared to generate them, but rather to the latent dream's thoughts (p. 580), and were reflective of the conflict (either libidinal stasis, or later a signal of danger) between the unconscious wish and the forces of censorship.

This paper takes clinical examples to explore the idea that paintings made during the course of therapy may be used by the client's defence mechanisms so that the picture and picture-making process are utilised against expression of creativity. Myth, Mothering and Psychoanalysis

Does psychoanalysis have to begin and end in myth? Certainly one of its beginnings was in Freud's appeal to the gripping power of Sophocles' Oedipus Rex as evidence of the ubiquity of murderous rivalry with the father for love of the mother. But his use of myth was as polemic - to underwrite the discoveries of his self-analysis and clinical practice. Christiane Olivier's use of myth in Jocasta's Children is similarly polemical. But whereas Freud emphasised the sexual desire of children and fathers, Olivier uses myth - that of Jocasta - to underscore her observations as a psychoanalyst of the formative influence on human psychology of the mother's desire.

Evocatively and compellingly she traces her patients' and her own sexual malaise to the different early experience of men and women when, she claims, sons but not daughters are sexually desired by the mother. This initially flatters the boy's narcissism until the anal stage when boy begins a life-long struggle with women for apparently wanting to wrest his penis from him just as his mother seemingly wanted his penis along with his faeces when he was a toddler. Hence, Olivier goes on, men's endless attempt to escape women's clinging - Jocasta's embrace - through language and sex.

This struggle, she asserts, is made all the more intense because the very mothering that provokes men's flight from women provokes women demandingly to cling to men. So much have women been starved of the mother's desire along with her milk, insists Olivier, that they avidly look to men and to their children to gratify their otherwise unslaked desire. No wonder they keep child care to themselves. No wonder men are only too happy to let them do so. For they can thereby keep at bay the mothering that seemingly so threatens to engulf them. Nevertheless, urges Oliver, only through men participating equally in early child care will the ill-effects of the mother's desire - or of its lack - be offset by that of the father. Meanwhile, she argues, men and women can escape Jocasta's thrall by drawing instead on a good image of the mother. This is where the analyst comes in, she concludes, through helping to make conscious the unconscious conflict underlying the sexism that feminism so deplores.

Austin Case

Austin Case  

In continuing the vitality and development of Freud's and Klein's ideas the three clinical papers written by Ronald Brittan, Michael Feldman and Edna O'Shaughnessy expand on the Oedipus Complex today as seen by post-Kleinian psychoanalysts. It is a much-needed and worthwhile contribution to understanding current Kleinian clinical work. Hanna Segal writes the introduction emphasising that one of ‘Klein's earliest discoveries was that of early forms of the superego and of the Oedipus complex before genital primacy’. These primitive forms of the oedipus complex showed that pregenital did not necessarly mean pre-oedipal. All the authors use Bion's concept of the container and the contained as the prototype for perceptions and experiences of the relationships between the parents. Bion's influence is seen in thinking as well. Thinking is based on making links including the links between parents. Patients with the severe disturbances used in the clinical examples of early Oedipal disturbances find these links particularly unbearable. The three authors bring needed and important clinical examples of these primitive and psychotic forms of the Oedipal complex. Following the preface is a reprint of Melanie Klein's The Oedipus Complex in the Light of Early Anxieties (1945), recognising the base for the contributions that follow.

In Chapter Two ‘The Missing Link: Parental Sexuality in the Oedipus Complex’ Ronald Brittan emphasises the Oedipus complex developing hand-in-hand with the evolution of the depressive position - ‘the working through of one entails the working through of the other’. He further brings out ‘if the encounter with the parental relationship starts to take place at a time when the individual has not established a securely based maternal object, the Oedipus situation appears in analysis only in primitive form and is not immediately recognizable as the classic Oedipus Complex’. A clinical example of this is given along with an example of what he calls an Oedipal illusion. The Oedipal illusion is developmentally a later phenomenon than the primitive wiping out of the parental relationship. The case presented shows how these illusions allow the parental relationship to be known but its full significance is evaded. The boundary between parental relationship and the parent-child relationship is not allowed.

Edith Hargreaves

Edith Hargreaves

Edith Hargreaves  

The work of Betty Joseph, along with that of Bion, Rosenfeld and Segal, has profoundly, though in her case perhaps rather quietly, influenced a new generation of Kleinian psychoanalysts. With them she has developed and extended Klein's concept of projective identification and its implications for analytic thinking about the use of transference and counter-transference in clinical practice.

Joseph's distinctive contribution lies in her unflinching interest and openness to the most daunting and apparently intractable clinical dilemmas, in which the patient seems emotionally inaccessible and the analysis fails to progress, and in her refinement of a technique which, she argues, offers the analyst more hope of making meaningful contact with the patient.

In Joseph's vivid and sensitive evocation of the clinical situation the reader, whatever his theoretical orientation, will recognise himself and his patients, and the struggles they are engaged in to understand and remain in contact with painful experience. Kleinian, or non-Kleinian, one cannot, I believe, fail to feel helped by her approach to take a fresh look at one's work.

The book is divided into four sections, ‘Beginnings’, ‘Breakthrough’, ‘Consolidation’ and ‘Recent Developments’, each containing several papers presented in the order in which they were written and representing stages in the evolution of Joseph's ideas.

In their introductions the editors, Spillius and Feldman, help the reader to trace the development of Joseph's ideas and to identify the major themes which constitute her unique contribution to modern psycho-analytic practice. These they outline as:

The patient's need to maintain his or her existing psychic equilibrium despite the conscious wish to change

Psychic change and the forces which promote or militate against it

The evolution of a technique which takes account of the above, described by the editors as the attempt to provide, within the analytic setting:

a precise working out of the way the patient's ideas and feelings, conscious and unconscious about himself, his analyst and the analytic relationship are lived out in the session. She argues that the way in which the patient consciously and unconsciously structures the analytic relationship makes apparent the nature of his internal world, which itself is the product of his complex history. Increasingly she has moved away from making global, explanatory interpretations, towards making more limited and precise descriptions to the patient of how, at a given moment, he sees the analyst, himself, and what is happening between them … In her view such immediate interpretations, even though apparently so limited, offer the best hope of working towards psychic change.

R. D. Laing

Joseph Berke

Joseph Berke

41 Weston Park, London N8

Joseph Berke  

I would like to say a few words about a recent event. I refer, sadly, to the death of Dr R D Laing. Dr Laing, Ronnie as he was affectionately known, was an inspiration to me personally and had a seminal influence on the founding and development of the Arbours Association. I would not like this occasion to pass without considering the impact of his work.

Ronnie put the person back into patient. He humanised the practice of psychiatry at a time when psychiatry meant constraint and punishment. He allowed us to see that something intelligible and vibrant exists in even the most bizarre, regressed and seemingly ‘crazy’ man or woman. I think, in particular, of Mary Barnes who is here with us tonight. Previously she had been treated, or should I say, mistreated with a bewildering array of medications and incarcerations and was in great danger of being confirmed in the career of a chronic mental patient. Having met Laing, she felt sufficiently understood, and thereby gained the strength to pass through a number of terrifying but ultimately healing regressions.

Ronnie was not the first healer to make madness and the process of going mad comprehensible. One only has to think of Sigmund Freud or Melanie Klein to name but two of his predecessors. Nonetheless Ronnie brought a breath of fresh air to the view prevalent in the 1950's and, unfortunately, still all to prevalent today that severe mental disorders can be ascribed solely to aberrant genes or a bad biochemistry.

One way he accomplished this was by his descriptive brilliance. Like Freud he was masterly in deploying a rich vocabulary to bring to life the dry bones of psychic pain and psychotic states. In other words he could flesh out the existential realities of the most regressed, irrational and, for that matter, irate human being. But more than a great dramatist Ronnie was also a great decoder of the human condition. As the playright David Edgar points out, he was able to make sense of schizophrenia - schizophrenic behaviour, the schizophrenic experience because he understood that mad people talk and live within metaphors. And he also knew that people do this in order to protect themselves from the dangers of living within a particular familial or social context. For example, one young woman was diagnosed as schizophrenic because she insisted on calling herself by the name of Taylor. Laing pointed out that the name reflected her experience, someone who was cut up, shaped and sown up by her parents. The reality was that she saw herself and was indeed treated as a tailored maid.

Healing, Exorcism and Object Relations Theory

Nathan Field

Nathan Field

14 Talbot Road, Highgate, London N6

Nathan Field  

From the earliest years of the psychoanalytic movement analysts have inclined to be either healers or exorcists. Jung, Ferençzi, Rank and Reich seem to speak with the characteristic voice of the healer. There is an implicit trust in the healing power of relationship, an emphasis on the patient's creative potential, a readiness to engage. Whereas those analysts, like Karl Abraham, who followed Freud's advocacy of analytic detachment, maintain a greater distance between themselves and their patient while focussing on the negative aspects of the infantile psyche. This tradition set the style of the classical analytic approach rigorously maintained by Melanie Klein and her followers. The Kleinian school actively challenges resistance, manipulation, seduction and all the carefully hidden expressions of negative transference. In their determination to ‘name the devils’ and their readiness to confront them, they, like Davanloo, take the characteristic stance of the exorcist.

While healing and exorcism are very different modes of functioning, it would be a false simplification to see them as mutually exclusive. The shaman, in reclaiming the lost soul, must at the same time do battle with the devils that hold it captive. The exorcist, even as he drives out the demons, prays earnestly for the soul of the sinner. An object relations analyst must be capable of controntation when the occasion warrants; equally the classical analyst heals through sensitive understanding and the maintenance of safe analytic boundaries. Healing alone will fail where no attempt is made to purge the patient of his bad inner objects. But, more fundamentally, the whole therapeutic enterprise is meaningful only to the degree that a truly human connection has been established. The difficulty is to move freely between the two modes and to see them as complementary aspects of a single process.

Giuseppina Antinucci-Mark  

Becoming a therapist is a complex process, much more so if the therapist is a foreigner who practises abroad and not in his/her mother-tongue. In this paper I try to analyse some aspects of that process drawing on my personal experience as a trainee-analysand and as a psychotherapist. Clinical examples are given of the anxieties, defences and the creative uses of being a bilingual clinician. A parallel is drawn between some of the dynamics within the patient/therapist couple and Thomas Mann's analysis of foreignness in The Magic Mountain.

This paper explores issues raised in psychotherapeutic work with adult survivors of child sexual abuse. An analysis is made of the long-term psychological effects of the trauma and the psychic dilemma as experienced by the patient. Four themes relevant to the therapist are explored: the problems raised by the seduction theory, the dangers of interpreting the patient's experience as fantasy, the potential abuse of power and control, and the implications of the gender of the therapist.

Joan Schachter

Joan Schachter

Joan Schachter  

This book contains many interesting and provocative ideas, but I found it a difficult book to read (in contrast to his previous book The Shadow of the Object), particularly the first part. It seemed to me that Bollas' literary and intellectual style at times rendered his meaning obscure and elusive, provoking irritation in the reader. There is also quite a bit of repetition which arises partly out of the fact that each chapter was originally a talk given whilst the author was working in the USA. I thought it fair to reveal my bias at the beginning of the review so that the reader can bear it in mind.

Bollas states in his introduction that this book is an effort to think about that aspect of the patient's use of the analytic situation, akin to play, which is an elaboration of latent elements of the personality. In the first part of the book he aims to develop a theory of Winnicott's concept of the true self. Bollas calls the true self (the inherited potential which depends on maternal care of its evolution) the idiom of the personality. He postulates an urge to use objects through which to articulate the true self which he terms the destiny drive. I remain uncertain how much these new terms really contribute to our thinking or whether they promote woolly quasi-philosophical thinking about the development of the self.

Bollas aligns himself with other Independent Group Analysts (Balint, Winnicott, Milner) in focusing on the way in which the analytic encounter may or may not facilitate the development of authentic self experience. He contrasts the deconstructive elements of the analyst's function (interpreting the latent content) with what he calls the constructive elements, in which the patient is facilitated to use the analyst in order to elaborate the true self. He gives several clinical vignettes to illustrate this. His interest in the use the patient is making of the analyst's personality extends beyond the transferencecountertransference paradigm. He demonstrates how and when he functions differently in order to provide himself as the ‘to be destroyed object’ for the patient. These clinical illustrations are rather lively and thought provoking and quite revealing of Bollas's style as an analyst. Writing so openly about his technique he renders himself vulnerable to criticisms of acting out in the countertransference; but I think this merits more serious consideration. Some of his examples were reminiscent of the papers of Symington and Coltart, who describe ‘actions’ they took in order to break out of an impasse.

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley

Haya Oakley  

The aim of this lengthy book as declared on its sleeve by the author, Dr Joseph Berke, is ‘to develop a detailed understanding of our capacity for destruction, as well as for making good’. What is true for the individual psyche, claims the author, is also the case when looking at cultural, social, political and economical phenomena. He puts forward the relatively straightforward thesis that inherent in our culture, as in the psyche, is a conflict between life and death, good and evil, light and darkness. For the individual a denial of the negative, dark, destructive elements will bring about severe psychopathology. When such a denial is done by society, grave cultural, economical and political calamities will follow, some of an international magnitude. Only full recognition of both good and evil, and the chance to repair the real as well as the imaginary damage caused by evil, would restore the health of the individual, mitigate the cultural tyranny, create a more benign culture and presumably bring peace and harmony to the world.

The book is in three parts. Part One explores the nature of malice and its various representations. ‘Envy, greed and jealousy are the negative constituents of character and culture’ (p. 268). This is done through examining the myth of the evil eye, the concepts of penis envy, narcissism, womb envy and the attacking of the breast. Myths, folklore and social behaviour theories have recognised Evil and its expressions as a permanent feature of culture, even before the mind was monopolised by the specialists. The common wisdom in relation to them was passed on through tales, poems and sayings (p. 44):

Envy cuts its own throat.

Envy devours its own master.

The envious man injures no one so much as himself.

With the help of sometimes tragic, sometimes humorous anecdotes, ranging from Paul McCartney to Siriono of Bolivia, Berke claims that most societies have developed ways of dealing with the damage caused by envy. The fear of success is apparently the fear of the envy success may bring upon the successful.
